# skill: prime-context-with-indirect-prompts-and-compound
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/prime-context-with-indirect-prompts-and-compound.md
========================================================================

---
name: Prime context with indirect prompts and compound skills
description: >-
  Use this when researching, planning, prototyping, or architecting with pstack
  — especially to draw intent out of the agent (/teach, /how, /why, /recall),
  compound context across skills, or run /architect before large changes.
---
# Steps
1. Prime the agent's context window with high-quality context. Two common failure modes: (1) under/poorly specified intent; (2) not enough context to do the work correctly. Outcomes are better when agents get everything they need for a high-quality job.
2. Use the indirect prompt: instead of telling the agent exactly what you want, draw it out in its own words. Example after a Slack report:
   - `/poteto-mode read this slack thread. restate in your own words and in plain english what you think the underlying issue is`
   - Effects: compresses noisy conversation into a structured problem statement; catches misunderstandings before code; avoids leading the agent with your own (possibly wrong) assumptions.
3. Build shared mental models with `/teach`, which under the hood calls `/how` and `/why`:
   - `/how` — traces runtime mechanics; assesses subsystem complexity; if multi-directory/service, spawns parallel explorer agents on fast efficient models (e.g. Grok). Example: `/how is virtualization implemented?`
   - `/why` — investigates motivation/intent; queries historical evidence in parallel across sources named in the extract: Git history and PR review comments, Linear tickets, Notion design docs, Slack conversations, Datadog monitors, Sentry errors, code lineage, analytics warehouse events. Example: `/why are we still stuck an old version of node.js?`
   - `/teach` example: `/teach me why you implemented it this way and not <other way>. what were the tradeoffs you made and why?` — restating for you also forces the agent to back claims with data/code.
4. Recover cross-conversation context with `/recall` (past transcripts as gold mine). Example: `/recall the work i did yesterday on virtualization and then read this bug report on slack`
5. Plan through code / working backwards (readme-driven for shared packages): craft the readme/tutorial first (developer-experience hat), then work backwards to implementation. Use `/technical-writing` (Diátaxis: Tutorial, How-to guide, Reference, Explanation) plus `/unslop` for readable docs. A written plan gives agents a concrete target to check work against.
6. Compound context in design-phase prompts. Example multi-step compound from the extract:
   - (1) `/recall my work fixing virtualization bugs and perf issues from the past 7 days. use /how and /why to understand how our current virtualization implementation works.`
   - (2) `then use /poteto-mode planning and /technical-writing to come up with a new virtualization engine that categorically eliminates flickering and jittering. let's start by writing a tutorial on how i would use this new package to virtualize a React app`
   - (3) `after you write the plan, /teach me and prove to me why this new approach is superior to our current engine` (proof relies on high-quality verification skills)
7. Prefer empirical prototyping over accepting the first design or overcooking abstract plans. `/poteto-mode` playbooks are reference files conditionally loaded by task type (not separate skills). Examples:
   - `/poteto-mode prototype a few options for the new dropdown menu`
   - `/poteto-mode fix this bug`
   - `/poteto-mode eval this skill change`
   - Visual/feature prototype: `/poteto-mode prototype a few options for <feature request>. use /control-app and take videos/screenshots for me to review and choose from` (`/control-app` = verification skill from Pt.1). Throwaway sketches or switcher variants; drive with `/control-app`; screenshots; measure timing/layout.
8. For bigger changes, use `/architect` phases as described:
   1. Ground the problem — `/how` and `/why` over affected systems
   2. Sketch — architecture arena; independent candidate runners in parallel (often different model families); each drafts usage sketch, core types, public signatures, concise rationale; evaluate interface depth, failure modes on weak models, design red flags catalog
   3. Cross-judge and synthesize — different model than main agent; strict rubric
   4. Implement against the sketch — replace placeholders; surface unexpected params/state discrepancies
   5. Scrap when the design is wrong — throw away and start over if empirical proof shows architecture wrong (e.g. same workaround across unrelated call sites; types need `any` or forced casts)
   - Prompt form: `/architect this new <feature request>`
9. If you need a tactical planning doc after a design you're happy with: `/poteto-mode turn this design into a plan` (multi-phase planning playbook; every task structured around proof and verification — tests alone are not sufficient; verify by actually running the code). Plans checked by an automated structure/formatting script; execute item by item with small self-contained PRs. For week-scale work, optionally commit plans temporarily then delete when done — [PLACEHOLDER: where plans live in your repo]. Do not keep plans permanently if that leaves confusion.
10. Example end-to-end prompts from the extract:
    - Ambiguous bug: `/poteto-mode investigate why background workers periodically fail with timeout errors. give me a breakdown of what we know, what data you used, and your best hypotheses.`
    - New service boundary: `/poteto-mode we need to add rate limiting for external webhooks. /architect this first, and answer any open questions with prototypes. let me review before proceeding.`
    - Multi-PR migration: `/poteto-mode create a plan to migrate our entire UI library to StyleX. break the migration into small, verifiable PRs. each PR must have its visual regression tests and live verification steps. i want the final result to be 100% identical compared to the original - bugs included`
    - Slack with enough context: `/poteto-mode do it` or `/poteto-mode repro this with /control-app. if it repros on main, fix it and show me a video as proof` (many skills already auto-used by `/poteto-mode`)

## Anti-patterns
- Micromanaging exact implementation when frontier models can solve better given goals and freedom.
- Stating your own assumptions/hypotheses first and leading the agent down a wrong path.
- Accepting the agent's first design without prototyping / measuring.
- Overcooking abstract plans without empirical evidence; reviewing abstract plans adversarially (agents hallucinate theoretical risks and invent edge cases for problems that will never happen).
- Using harness "plan modes" that over-specify implementation details and under-specify everything else.
- Treating lengthy abstract plans as progress (illusion of productivity without substance).

## Source
- https://x.com/poteto/status/2097732320606507506, @poteto, Wed Sep 09 17:02:13 +0000 2026 (2026-09-10 03:02 AEST)


========================================================================
# skill: produce-kurzgesagt-style-explainers-with-approva
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/produce-kurzgesagt-style-explainers-with-approva.md
========================================================================

---
name: Produce Kurzgesagt-style explainers with approval gates
description: >-
  Use this when you want a coding agent to produce an original 2D animated
  explainer in a Kurzgesagt-inspired visual style, with script and storyboard
  approval before any asset spend, layered artwork, narration sync, contact
  sheets and preview clips.
---
# Goal
Run research, script, storyboard, original illustration, motion, voice, sound and render as one directed workflow, without copying a channel's characters, logos or scenes, and without spending on assets until script and storyboard are approved.

# Inputs
- <TOPIC>, or a request for three fact-checked topic suggestions
- Format: 55–65 second explainer (default 60 s) or 90–110 second promotional video
- A reference video to analyse for visual language, not to copy
- An image model that supports reference images and high-resolution output (the prompt names GPT Image 2 as one option)
- A text-to-speech service (the prompt names ElevenLabs or Kokoro)
- An environment that can run Python, install packages, use Chromium and render video

# Steps
1. Paste the director prompt below into Claude Opus (the model named in the post) or an equivalent coding agent that can research, generate images, write code and render.
2. Attach a reference video. The prompt contains a shot-by-shot reading of the author's ~107 s, 1280×720, 60 FPS reference with no audio. If you attach a different reference, replace that section with your own analysis. Don't invent narration or sound that isn't on the file.
3. Answer the intake questions: topic, format, image model, voice service, and whether the environment can run Python and render.
4. Stop at the complete script and timestamped shot plan. No assets or spend until you approve both.
5. After approval, require layered assets (background, midground, foreground, separate characters and props), a character sheet, two contact sheets and preview clips before the final render. Narration must match the timestamps.
6. Characters and worlds must be original. No copying Kurzgesagt's (or any channel's) characters, logos, artwork or scenes.
7. Fact-check script claims against sources before render. Reject any claim from the agent that it rendered or verified something it didn't produce.

# The director prompt (verbatim from the post; list items joined onto lines)

```
<ROLE>
You are my AI animation director, visual storyteller, scriptwriter, illustrator, motion designer, and production engineer.
Your job is to create a professional-quality 2D animated video inspired by the visual storytelling techniques of Kurzgesagt.
I have attached a reference video. Analyze it before doing anything else.
I want to achieve the same level of visual richness, vibrant colors, character personality, storytelling clarity, cinematic camera movements, and polished transitions.
Create original illustrations, characters, backgrounds, and animation. Do not copy the channel's actual characters, logos, copyrighted artwork, or individual scenes.
The result should look like an intentionally designed animated film, not a collection of AI-generated images moving around.
Your responsibilities include: Research and fact-checking; Scriptwriting; Storyboarding; Character design; Background illustration; Asset generation; Character rigging; Motion animation; Voiceover; Sound design; Editing; Rendering; Quality control.
Do not generate assets or spend money until I approve the script and storyboard.

<INPUTS>
First, ask me for:
Topic: What should the video explain? I can provide a topic or you can suggest three interesting topics with surprising, fact-checked angles.
Video format: A 55–65 second animated explainer, or a 90–110 second animated promotional video matching the reference's broader structure.
Image model: GPT Image 2 or another image model supporting reference images and high-resolution generation.
Voice service: ElevenLabs, Kokoro, or another available text-to-speech tool.
Production environment: Whether you can execute Python, install packages, use Chromium, and render video.
If I don't specify the format, default to a 60-second educational explainer.
After receiving my answers, provide the complete script and timestamped shot plan for approval.

<REFERENCE VIDEO ANALYSIS>
Study the attached video frame by frame.
Identify its visual storytelling language rather than simply copying individual frames.
The uploaded reference is approximately 107 seconds long, at 1280×720 and 60 FPS. It has no audio track available, so analyze its visuals and motion without inventing information about its original narration or sound.
Its visual structure includes:
0–27 seconds: Character-led animated opening. A dark blue and purple illustrated world featuring expressive geometric bird characters, mysterious glowing objects, colorful movement trails, and background environments filled with details.
27–63 seconds: Live-action product demonstration. Product close-ups, overhead desk compositions, real human interaction, colorful backdrops, and clean informational graphics.
63–76 seconds: High-energy laboratory animation. Bright blue scientific environments, large illustrated machinery, colorful containers, experiments, animated characters, and energetic transitions.
76–86 seconds: Product and feature presentation. Clear focal points, product compositions, colorful graphic accents, and simple feature highlights.
86–101 seconds: Rich animated world. Warm orange environments with stylized bird characters, machines, vegetation, architectural details, and multiple layers of action.
101–107 seconds: Final hero composition. A clean product-focused ending with strong visual hierarchy and a clear call to action.
Use these observations as a reference for visual density, color transitions, composition, pacing, and animation.
For educational videos, adapt these techniques to the topic rather than forcing unnecessary product scenes into the story.
Before proceeding, produce: A visual style analysis; A color palette with approximate HEX values; A reference contact sheet; A scene and transition breakdown; A motion and camera behavior summary; A proposed original character design system.

<VISUAL DIRECTION>
Output: 1920×1080, 16:9, 60 FPS.
Artwork generation: 3840×2160 where supported.
Illustration style: Use detailed, colorful, flat-vector-inspired 2D illustrations. Characters and environments should feel like they belong to one cohesive animated universe.
Characteristics: Smooth geometric shapes; Bold silhouettes; Minimal or no outlines; Solid colors with carefully chosen secondary shadow colors; Saturated colors balanced against darker backgrounds; Soft gradients only where appropriate; Layered environments; Expressive nonrealistic characters; Simplified faces with highly readable emotions; Detailed props built from simple shapes.
Avoid photorealism, anime aesthetics, generic 3D renders, glossy AI artwork, and inconsistent illustrations.
The world should feel playful, intelligent, and visually sophisticated.

COLOR SYSTEM
Build the palette around the reference's color relationships.
Suggested working colors:
- Deep backgrounds: #09134B, #180A59
- Royal blue: #243CDB
- Purple: #6535A8
- Teal and cyan: #22D7DA, #33B9D7
- Warm orange: #FF851D
- Pink accents: #ED4BA4
- Yellow highlights: #FFD244
- Light blue: #8CAAF7
Treat these as starting approximations, not exact sampled values.
Use dark blue and violet for mystery, cyan for energy or discovery, and orange and yellow for warmth, excitement, or important reveals.
Every scene should have a clear dominant color.
Do not randomly change palettes between shots.
Use color transitions to support the story.

<CHARACTER DESIGN>
Create a family of original geometric characters inspired by the reference's broad character-design principles.
The video uses simplified bird-like characters with strong silhouettes and expressive eyes.
Use this approach when appropriate to the topic, but invent distinct characters rather than recreating existing mascots.
Character characteristics: Large, simplified heads and bodies; Rounded or geometric silhouettes; Small wings or arms; Expressive eyes; Simple mouths or beaks; Short legs; Limited but expressive facial features; Highly readable body language; Contrasting body and accent colors.
Generate a consistent character sheet containing: Front view; Side view; Three-quarter view; Back view; Happy expression; Confused expression; Surprised expression; Worried expression; Walking pose; Pointing or gesturing pose.
Every character must remain visually consistent throughout the video.
Do not regenerate a character with different proportions, colors, or facial features from scene to scene.

CHARACTER ANIMATION
Animate characters using rigged body parts.
Separate assets when needed: Body; Head; Eyes; Eyelids; Mouth or beak; Wings or arms; Legs; Hands; Accessories.
Give characters natural illustrated motion.
Use: Head rotations of approximately ±3–8 degrees; Blinking every 2.5–4 seconds; Wing or arm gestures synchronized with narration; Slight body bobbing; Anticipation before significant movements; Squash and stretch; Subtle overshoot when landing; Small reaction delays; Expressive pose changes.
Characters should occasionally blink, point, turn, lean, jump, walk, and react.
Their movements should reflect the narration.
Avoid repetitive looping motions that have no connection to the scene.

<ENVIRONMENT DESIGN>
Every scene should be a complete illustrated environment, not a flat background with disconnected objects.
Examples include: Futuristic laboratories; Alien planets; Microscopic biological worlds; Factories; Forests; Cities; Classrooms; Oceans; Space environments; Underground chambers; Historical locations.
The environment should match the subject.
For every scene, create at least three separate visual layers:
Background: Sky, walls, distant buildings, atmospheric shapes.
Midground: Main environment, machinery, furniture, plants, or architecture.
Foreground: Characters, close objects, particles, and framing elements.
Add appropriate environmental details.
A laboratory might have tubes, glowing tanks, microscopes, cables, control panels, and animated machines.
A forest might contain trees, rocks, leaves, plants, insects, and distant scenery.
Every important object should contribute to the storytelling.
Avoid clutter that distracts from the focal point.

<CINEMATIC CAMERA SYSTEM>
The reference uses motion to make flat illustrations feel cinematic.
Recreate that approach with a virtual 2D camera.
Use:
Slow push-ins: Gradually move closer to important subjects.
Pullbacks: Reveal the scale of an environment.
Horizontal pans: Follow moving characters or reveal new information.
Vertical camera movements: Show height, depth, and scale.
Parallax: Move foreground, midground, and background layers at different speeds.
Tracking shots: Follow characters through illustrated environments.
Crash zooms: Emphasize surprising discoveries.
Wide establishing shots: Introduce a new location.
Use movement deliberately.
Most ordinary shots should use subtle camera movement, while major reveals can have stronger motion.
Keep all backgrounds large enough to prevent empty borders.
Do not apply the same zoom effect to every scene.

<ANIMATION LANGUAGE>
This is extremely important.
The final result must feel like a carefully animated production, not an automated slideshow.
Use these animation principles:
1. Anticipation. Before a major action, create a small opposite movement. A character preparing to jump should crouch first. A machine activating should briefly compress or shake.
2. Squash and stretch. Important objects should compress and expand during movement. Maintain consistent visual volume.
3. Overshoot. Objects should travel slightly past their final position before settling. Use spring easing for playful motion.
4. Follow-through. Character wings, accessories, plants, and other secondary elements should continue moving briefly after the main action stops.
5. Staggered animation. Do not animate everything simultaneously. Have objects enter in sequence to direct attention.
6. Secondary motion. Use small environmental animations: Floating particles; Blinking lights; Moving machinery; Gently swaying plants; Drifting smoke; Rotating objects; Rippling liquids; Glowing energy.
7. Smooth transformations. Where possible, morph simple geometric shapes between related objects. Use shape interpolation rather than unnecessarily cutting away.
8. Animation timing. Render at 60 FPS. Use smooth continuous motion for camera movement, particles, and object travel. Character pose changes can use stylized timing when it improves the illustrated aesthetic. Avoid robotic linear interpolation.

<STORY STRUCTURE>
DEFAULT: 60-SECOND EDUCATIONAL EXPLAINER
0–4 seconds — VISUAL HOOK. Begin with something surprising. Show an unusual situation or a visually impossible-looking scenario. Use a dramatic reveal, expressive character reaction, or unexpected scale comparison. The opening should make the viewer want an explanation.
4–11 seconds — ESTABLISH THE QUESTION. Introduce the main question. Use a wide illustrated environment. Show why the question matters through visible actions. Avoid lengthy introductions.
11–20 seconds — SETUP. Explain the necessary background. Introduce relevant characters, environments, and concepts. Use physical objects to represent abstract ideas.
20–35 seconds — THE EXPLANATION. Explain the main mechanism through 3–5 connected visual actions. Show cause and effect. Move between appropriate environments. Use diagrams only when they genuinely improve understanding.
35–47 seconds — CONSEQUENCES. Show what happens because of the mechanism. Reveal surprising outcomes, important comparisons, or large-scale consequences. Use visual reactions and animated transformations.
47–57 seconds — THE TWIST. Introduce the most surprising insight. Connect it directly to the opening question. Use the strongest visual sequence near the end.
57–65 seconds — CONCLUSION. Deliver a satisfying answer. Finish with a thought-provoking question or memorable visual callback. Avoid an abrupt ending.
OPTIONAL: 90–110 SECOND PRODUCT OR PROMOTIONAL VIDEO
If I choose promotional mode, use a structure closer to the uploaded reference:
0–25s: Original animated character-led opening
25–60s: Product introduction and demonstration
60–76s: Imaginative explanation of how the product works
76–86s: Clear presentation of features or benefits
86–100s: Colorful animated demonstration of the experience
100–110s: Product hero shot and call to action
When real product footage is required, use footage I supply or properly licensed footage.
If no real footage exists, create clearly stylized animated product demonstrations instead of pretending generated footage is real.

<SCENE GENERATION>
Before generating images, create a complete shot plan.
For every scene, specify: Scene number; Start and end time; Exact narration; Visual description; Dominant color; Background assets; Character assets; Foreground props; Character movement; Camera movement; Transition type; Sound effects; Asset-generation prompt.
Generate the necessary assets separately.
Do not make one complete flattened image and simply zoom into it.
Create layered artwork so individual objects can move.
ASSET GENERATION RULES
Generate background plates without foreground characters.
Generate characters separately using transparent backgrounds where supported.
Use chroma green (#00B140) when transparency is unreliable.
Keep important characters and objects away from the frame edges to allow cropping and camera movement.
Generate individual props as isolated assets.
Avoid baking text into AI-generated artwork.
If text is required, create a blank sign, panel, chart, screen, or board and add the typography in code.
Use high-resolution assets to avoid blurry edges.
Maintain a consistent perspective within each scene.

<PROGRAMMATIC CHARACTER CUTOUTS>
Use Python, Pillow, and OpenCV to prepare character sprites.
For chroma-green images:
Start with: G - max(R,B) > 40
Compare against the median background green.
Select background-colored pixels connected to the image border.
Do not remove interior green pixels automatically.
Generate a clean alpha mask.
Add a 2-pixel feathered edge.
Suppress green spill around the character.
Separate body components at natural joints for animation.
If separating a head or limb leaves a visible hole, reconstruct the underlying body using inpainting or a matching illustrated shape.
Inspect every sprite before animation.
Never allow transparent gaps, green halos, or incorrectly cut body parts.

<VOICEOVER>
Use my selected narration service.
The delivery should be: Clear; Curious; Intelligent; Conversational; Expressive without exaggeration; Appropriately paced for educational storytelling.
Use an original or properly authorized voice.
Do not impersonate a specific channel narrator without permission.
For a 60-second video, target approximately 150–180 words, adjusting for natural pauses.
Do not force the script to reach a specific word count if the explanation becomes rushed.
Generate a complete narration take.
Remove unnecessarily long pauses while preserving natural delivery.
Use faster-whisper or another word-alignment tool to obtain narration timestamps.
Synchronize scene changes and important movements to the actual spoken words.
If speech alignment has errors, correct them before animation.

<MOTION ENGINE>
Build the animation using HTML Canvas, JavaScript, SVG, or another suitable deterministic rendering system.
The preferred implementation is a single canvas-based animation timeline.
Expose: seek(t); READY; END; EV
Where:
seek(t) renders any requested timestamp
READY indicates that assets are loaded
END contains the final timeline duration
EV contains narration and animation timing events
Each rendered frame should be a deterministic function of time.
Create reusable functions for: Character movement; Head rotation; Eye blinking; Limb animation; Squash and stretch; Object entrance; Object rotation; Parallax; Camera movement; Particles; Glow; Wipe transitions; Shape morphing.
MOTION BEHAVIOR
Use easing curves, springs, and Bézier paths.
Avoid a uniform mechanical movement speed.
Characters should accelerate and decelerate naturally.
Large objects should feel heavier than small ones.
Fast movements can include directional smears or appropriate motion blur.
Apply camera transformations consistently across all layers.
Keep character rigs stable when rotating or scaling.

<TRANSITIONS>
Use varied transitions inspired by the reference's overall pacing.
Hard cuts: For clear changes in place or idea.
Whip pans: For energetic movement between related settings.
Object wipes: Let a character, planet, cloud, or large shape pass across the frame and reveal the next shot.
Color wipes: Fill the screen with a dominant color that becomes the next environment.
Scale transitions: Zoom through an object into a new world.
Shape morphs: Transform one illustrated object into another.
Bright flashes: Reserve for exceptional reveals.
Avoid random transitions.
Every transition should serve the visual narrative.

<TEXT AND TYPOGRAPHY>
Keep typography clean, bold, and readable.
Use fonts such as Montserrat, Poppins, or another suitable modern geometric sans-serif.
Use text sparingly.
Prefer visual explanations over full-screen paragraphs.
Text may appear on: Signs; Machines; Labels; Charts; Screens; Illustrated documents; Purpose-built title compositions.
Animate text using: Scale pops; Spring movement; Staggered word entrances; Slide-ins; Shape reveals.
Keep titles visually distinct from ordinary labels.
Avoid covering important characters with text.
Do not add continuous burned-in subtitles unless requested.

<TOOLS AND WORKFLOW>
Use the following tools when available: Python for automation; OpenCV for image and frame processing; Pillow for sprites and alpha masks; FFmpeg for rendering and encoding; Playwright with Chromium for browser-based frame rendering; NumPy and SciPy for calculations; librosa for audio analysis; faster-whisper for narration timestamps; SVG or Canvas for animation.
Before production: Check the installed tools. Identify missing dependencies. Install missing packages if permitted. Report what was installed. Confirm the available rendering environment.
If the environment cannot render the requested animation, do not pretend it can.
Provide the executable project files and the remaining production steps instead.

<RENDERING>
Render the finished animation at: Resolution: 1920×1080; Frame rate: 60 FPS; Codec: H.264; Encoder: libx264; Quality: CRF 16–18; Pixel format: yuv420p.
Use motion blur selectively for fast movement when supported.
Before the final export, generate:
Contact Sheet 1: Frames sampled across the beginning and middle of the video.
Contact Sheet 2: Frames sampled across the middle and ending.
Use at least 16 frames per sheet.
Inspect both sheets.
Fix: Inconsistent character designs; Incorrect proportions; Empty background areas; Broken transparency; Strange facial expressions; Text overflow; Missing props; Unnatural camera crops; Black frame borders; Excessively static compositions.
Also inspect short preview clips, because contact sheets alone cannot reveal timing or motion problems.

<SOUND DESIGN>
Create a polished educational documentary mix.
Use licensed or royalty-free music and effects.
Music should feel curious, adventurous, and slightly cinematic.
Match musical energy to the narrative.
Suggested effects: Soft pops for appearing objects; Whooshes for transitions; Sparkles for discoveries; Mechanical sounds for animated machines; Soft impact sounds for landings; Ambient sounds matching the environment; Brief musical accents for surprising reveals.
Never overwhelm the narration.
Use ducking or volume automation during spoken sections.
Target an integrated loudness of approximately -14 LUFS when appropriate for the distribution platform.
Avoid abrupt audio cuts.

<QUALITY CONTROL>
Before delivering the final video, verify:
VISUALS: Every scene uses the same illustration language. Character proportions and colors remain consistent. The environments feel detailed and intentional. There are no AI-generated visual artifacts. The video does not rely on static image zooms.
ANIMATION: Characters move naturally. Actions match narration. Movement uses appropriate easing. Transitions are visually coherent. There are no unexpected single-frame jumps.
STORY: The hook is clear. Every scene contributes to the explanation. The facts are accurate and sourced. The video delivers on its opening promise.
AUDIO: Narration is clear. Audio and visuals are synchronized. Effects are placed correctly. Music doesn't overpower speech.
EXPORT: The video plays correctly from beginning to end. No frames are missing. No assets appear blurred or distorted. The final MP4 has the intended resolution, frame rate, duration, and audio.
Fix problems before delivering.

<NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES>
Do not use a generic AI slideshow approach.
Do not use one flattened image for an entire animated scene.
Do not randomly change character designs.
Do not copy recognizable Kurzgesagt characters, logos, artwork, or exact compositions.
Do not make every scene look identical.
Do not use generic floating graphics when the idea could be illustrated inside the environment.
Do not move objects without purpose.
Do not ignore animation timing.
Do not generate unreadable text inside images.
Do not sacrifice factual accuracy for dramatic storytelling.
Do not claim to have rendered or verified assets that have not been produced.
Do not spend money or generate final assets without my approval.
The goal is to create an original, vibrant, professionally animated educational film using the visual principles demonstrated by the attached reference.
Prioritize visual storytelling, expressive character animation, coherent art direction, and polished motion.
```

# Success check
- A script and timestamped shot plan were approved before any asset generation.
- Characters match the character sheet in every scene.
- Artwork is layered, not one flattened image with a zoom.
- Narration matches shot timestamps.
- Two contact sheets and preview clips exist; no copied channel characters or logos appear.

# Failure modes
- The post's "killed Kurzgesagt style" and "15M+ subscribers / $0 extra" lines are promotional and unverified.
- The built-in reference analysis pulls toward that reference's structure, including product-demo segments. For a pure explainer, the prompt already says not to force product scenes.
- Image models drift character design between shots unless you keep a character sheet and reject mismatches.
- Chroma-key cutouts can leave green halos or holes at joints; inspect every sprite.
- The prompt's motion engine line read "Expose: (t)" in the source; it is shown here as seek(t), which the next lines define. (added, not in source)

# Anti-patterns
- Generating assets before script and storyboard approval.
- Copying the reference channel's mascots or specific scenes.
- Baking text into generated artwork instead of adding type in code.
- Accepting a claimed render or fact-check that didn't happen.
- Using this instead of the motion-graphics skill when you want HTML or React video (HyperFrames, Remotion) rather than this illustration-and-composite pipeline.

# Source
F*ck Scales (@fuckscales), https://x.com/fuckscales/status/2118801134924288456, 2026-11-06. A single Claude Opus prompt by the author. Inspired by Kurzgesagt-style techniques; not affiliated with that channel.

---
name: Pull leads from SEO/AEO via GSC striking-distance queries
description: >-
  Use this when turning Google Search Console into SEO/AEO leads: export
  Queries, pull bottom-of-funnel terms in positions 4–20, pick pages to push
  into the top 3–5, then use Claude + an AI Search checklist to prioritize and
  ship ranking-factor updates.
---
# Pull leads from SEO/AEO via GSC striking-distance queries

Turn Google Search Console into a lead pipeline: export query rankings, pull bottom-of-funnel queries in positions **4–20**, pick pages to push into positions **1–5** (ideally top 3), then use Claude + an AI Search checklist to prioritize on-page work and ship changes.

## Inputs

- Access to the site’s **Google Search Console**
- Claude (or equivalent) that can read a Google Sheet
- AI Search checklist: `[AI_SEARCH_CHECKLIST_URL]` (download from the source post’s first comment when available)
- Optional: known competitor and product names to bias matching

## Steps (follow exactly)

1. Open **Google Search Console**.

2. Go to **Performance** (upper-left).

3. Click the **Average position** box (top-middle) so it turns orange.

4. Select **28 days** (last month of rankings).

5. Click **Export** (upper-right) → **Google Sheets**.

6. Open the **Queries** tab of the Sheet:
   - Freeze row 1
   - Right-click the **Position** column → **Sort sheet A → Z**

7. Give the Sheet to Claude and run this prompt:

```text
Find all the bottom of funnel queries in the Queries tab of this sheet that are in positions 4 - 20. Specifically look for these types of queries:

[Competitor] Alternatives
[Competitor] vs [Competitor]
[Competitor] Review
Best [product] for X
How to export data from [Competitor]
[Software] for [role]
[Software] with an MCP connection
Home page
Services/Product pages

give me them here in a simple list
```

8. Choose the top keywords you’d want to rank higher for from that list. You will likely get **zero leads** unless you’re in positions **1–5** (ideally top 3). Then run:

```text
I'd like to improve my rankings for these pages:

- [PAGE 1]
- [PAGE 2]
- [PAGE 3]
- Etc.

Tell me which of these are going to be the easiest to improve My rankings on by analyzing who are the competitors currently above me in the SERP, the strength of their pages, and how easily I can update my page to have more ranking factors.

Use this AI Search checklist as a guide for what the perfectly optimized page would look like in an ideal world: [AI_SEARCH_CHECKLIST_URL]
```

Replace `[PAGE N]` with real URLs (or query→URL pairs). Attach/paste the checklist at `[AI_SEARCH_CHECKLIST_URL]` (original post: download link in the first comment).

9. Follow up with:

```text
give me the checklist items I would need to execute for the '[KEYWORD]' page in order to most likely increase my rankings, ordered by priority
```

10. Implement as many of those changes as possible.

11. Check **Google Search Console every day** for how rankings improved on that specific page.

## Success check

- Sheet exported with Average position on, last 28 days
- BOFU list filtered to positions 4–20
- Pages chosen for a top-3/5 push
- Prioritized checklist items shipped
- Daily GSC position checks running

## Anti-patterns

- Chasing top-of-funnel / non-converting queries
- Ignoring that leads cluster in positions 1–5
- Skipping SERP competitor analysis
- Shipping none of the checklist items
- Checking rankings rarely after changes
- Leaving the checklist link empty so Claude has no target model

## Source

- Method pasted by Steven (2026-09-25), from a practitioner who runs AI Search for 7–9 figure tech companies (e.g. beehiiv); claimed ~800k pipeline/quarter for their smallest client.
- Checklist download lives in the original post’s first comment → store as `[AI_SEARCH_CHECKLIST_URL]`.
- Related: [Add methodology scoring for AI information gain](sand-workflow:add-methodology-scoring-for-ai-information-gain)

# skill: research-first-landing-page-design
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/research-first-landing-page-design.md
========================================================================

---
name: Research-first landing page design
description: >-
  Use this when AI landing pages look generic — force a research report against
  real shipped references (Mobbin MCP or screenshots) before rebuild, then
  scoped fix passes.
---

# Research-first landing page design

You cannot prompt taste into a model. Show it what good looks like: research real shipped sites/apps first, approve a change report, then rebuild. Same model + same brief can look generic or premium depending only on what it studied before building.

Credit: workflow idea from Griffin Wooldridge (YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_EXYLmyFSA). Agency run / prompts from Prajwal Tomar.

## Core principle

- Do **not** connect references and say "make it better."
- Always: **research → report → wait for approval → build → annotate → mobile check → one scoped fix pass**.
- Taste words ("premium", "editorial", "magazine feel") alone produce the average of every site that called itself premium — the "AI premium" look.

## Build sheet (run every landing page)

```
Brief → Draft 1 → connect real references → research report (wait for it) → Draft 2 → annotate every change → mobile check → one fix pass on the weak section
```

Save the change-list patterns into project notes so the next client in the same category starts from taste, not zero.

---

## Exact prompts

Replace placeholders: `[PRODUCT]`, `[PAGE]`, `[CATEGORY]`, `[section]`, `[The one change]`.

### 1) Brief (Draft 1)

Use this structure (TripGlide example generalized):

```
Build a polished, responsive marketing website for [PRODUCT], a [one-line product description that names the category and positioning]. Sections: hero with a product UI preview of the app, how it works, curated destinations, itinerary feature, social proof, pricing, FAQ, footer. It should feel like a premium consumer [CATEGORY] brand: editorial typography, generous whitespace, subtle interactions, fully responsive. Generate your own imagery where needed.
```

TripGlide template (keep as reference; swap product details for new work):

```
Build a polished, responsive marketing website for TripGlide, a travel booking app that feels like a high-end digital travel magazine that happens to let you book. Sections: hero with a product UI preview of the app, how it works, curated destinations, itinerary feature, social proof, pricing, FAQ, footer. It should feel like a premium consumer travel brand: editorial typography, generous whitespace, subtle interactions, fully responsive. Generate your own imagery where needed.
```

### 2) Research report (REQUIRED before any redesign)

Connect Mobbin MCP (or attach screenshots — see Free path). Then send **exactly**:

```
Use this MCP to research design patterns for the current [PAGE] before making any changes. Study real, shipped [CATEGORY] and premium consumer brand websites and apps. Then write a report that: 1) identifies exactly where the current page feels generic or AI-generated, 2) summarizes the recurring patterns in the strongest real examples you found, 3) proposes a clearer visual direction for [PRODUCT], 4) lists every change you would make and why. Do not build anything until I approve the report.
```

TripGlide-filled example:

```
Use this MCP to research design patterns for the current TripGlide landing page before making any changes. Study real, shipped travel and premium consumer brand websites and apps. Then write a report that: 1) identifies exactly where the current page feels generic or AI-generated, 2) summarizes the recurring patterns in the strongest real examples you found, 3) proposes a clearer visual direction for TripGlide, 4) lists every change you would make and why. Do not build anything until I approve the report.
```

**Stop here.** Do not build until the human approves the report.

### 3) Approve + implement

```
Approved. Implement the report on the existing site.
```

### 4) Annotate every change

After Draft 2, go back to the report and check items off. Confirm the model used its own research (one dominant idea, specific decision support, real product evidence, no invented social proof/pricing unless real, etc.).

### 5) One fix pass (fence every post-rebuild change)

Never say "make the headlines less poetic" and let the model loose on the whole page. Scope every pass:

```
One fix pass, scoped to [section]. [The one change]. Change nothing else.
```

Example:

```
One fix pass, scoped to headline copy only. Rewrite the three serif and italic headlines to say something specific about the product. Change nothing else.
```

---

## What "AI premium" usually looks like (catch these in research)

- Decorations competing with no single organizing idea (tilted phone, floating reassurance card, GPS coordinates on photos, sparkles, sun icons, postcard numbers)
- Same headline formula every section (upright serif + sage italic phrase)
- Poetic copy that sounds on-brand but says nothing about what the product does
- Same hero photo reused across sections
- Unreadable product mockup labels (e.g. 6px type)
- Invented pricing and illustrative testimonials labeled as sample copy

## Patterns strong real references share (pull these into the report)

1. **One dominant visual idea** — one named stay / one product demo leads; everything else supports it
2. **Specific things people want** — properties, activities, dates, named places (not broad promises)
3. **Clear actions** — Book / Search / Save, labelled and placed where they belong
4. **Information next to the image** — cards help you decide something
5. **Big and small on purpose** — big editorial photos, compact practical details
6. **Real product evidence** — useful screens that show what the app does

---

## Client / agency extras (hold up on real projects)

1. **Design system first** — colours, type scale, spacing, components in one short doc the model reads before research. Without this, research pulls patterns that fight the brand.
2. **Research pass on the page** — the four-part report prompt above. Never "make it better." Always research, report, wait.
3. **Build → check mobile → second research pass on the one weak section** — there is always one. Research that section only; do not reopen the whole page.
4. **Save the patterns** — put the change list in project notes. Next client in the same category starts from those patterns.

---

## Free path (no Mobbin)

If you do not want to pay for Mobbin, the workflow still works — slower, narrower:

1. Open 10–12 real websites in your category that you actually admire.
2. Screenshot the hero, one content section, and the footer of each.
3. Drop them into the chat and run the same research prompt, replacing **"Use this MCP"** with **"study the attached screenshots."**
4. Everything else stays the same.

You lose breadth (600,000+ screens vs 12). You keep the part that matters: research before build.

---

## Mobbin setup note

- In ChatGPT: Apps → search Mobbin → add → sign in to authorize.
- Needs **Mobbin Pro or above** (free plan cannot connect MCP).
- Not sponsored; MCP lets the model browse instead of you.
- MCP can fail on first connect — reconnect and run again.
- Every search spends Mobbin AI credits (no published rate) — budget for it.

---

## Limits

- Report quality tracks the research prompt. Vague "research design patterns" → summary. The four-part prompt → actionable multi-item plan.
- Models love to rebuild the whole page when you asked for one section — **name the section in every fix prompt**.
- Model can copy one reference too closely — if the report keeps pointing at one site, tell it to widen the set before build.
- Images still need a pass (layout improves faster than photos).
- This is a **marketing site** workflow. For in-app screens, still start from a design system (research-first can be tried later for those too).
- Do not over-claim: flag mobile as risk until a real browser check; treat "generic" as design judgment, not AI-authorship detection.

---

## Anti-patterns

- Connecting Mobbin / dropping screenshots and saying "make it better" with no report
- Rebuilding the whole page to fix one weak section
- Leaving invented testimonials or fake pricing on a live client site
- Relying on taste words ("premium", "editorial") with no shipped references
- Skipping mobile check and the scoped fix pass

---

## Source

- Article / post: https://x.com/PrajwalTomar_/status/2100211370897920136
- Author: Prajwal Tomar (@PrajwalTomar_), Sep 16, 2026
- Griffin Wooldridge credit (originating demo): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L_EXYLmyFSA
- Newsletter patterns: https://theaiheadstart.com/

# skill: reverse-engineer-a-competitor-s-google-ads-weekl
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/reverse-engineer-a-competitor-s-google-ads-weekl.md
========================================================================

---
name: Reverse-engineer a competitor's Google Ads weekly
description: >-
  Use this when you already run Google Ads and want a weekly process to see who
  bids against you, what ads they run, which keywords they abandoned and where
  they are weak by location, then turn those gaps into campaign tests.
---
Weekly cadence. The source says a first pass takes about 10 minutes (author's claim, not verified).

You need your own Google Ads account for Auction Insights. Semrush Advertising Research (paid) is used in step 3.

## Inputs
- Your Google Ads account, with Auction Insights on the campaigns or ad groups that matter
- One competitor domain to start with, taken from Auction Insights
- Google Ads Transparency Center: https://adstransparency.google.com
- Semrush, if you use step 3

## Steps
1. **Auction Insights, not guesses.** Open Auction Insights on your top campaigns and ad groups. Note the exact domains bidding against you on your most valuable keywords, who outranks you, overlap rate and who is gaining impression share. That list is who you watch.
2. **Google Ads Transparency Center.** Enter the competitor's domain. Review the display, video, shopping and search ads running now. Study messaging, offers and creative approach. You are not copying; you are asking how they say things.
   - Generic ads: an opening to be more targeted.
   - Polished, targeted messaging: a clear strategy you need to match.
3. **Abandoned keywords in Semrush (paid).** Advertising Research > Position Changes > Lost. These are keywords they used to bid on and dropped. Possible reasons:
   - Not profitable for their model (you just saved time and money).
   - Budget moved elsewhere (a chance to take that share).
   - Dropped by mistake (the author says this happens more than people think).
   Also check which landing pages get the most paid traffic (homepage, collection pages, product pages, quiz funnels). That is their acquisition funnel. Ask where you can be better.
4. **Geographic gaps.** In the Transparency Center, use the location filter to compare countries, states and cities. Author's example: an aggressive free-gift offer in New Zealand but passive ads in Australia. Where they are weak is your opening.
5. **Stack the findings and look for what they are not doing.** Author's examples:
   - No video or image ads: test Demand Gen and Performance Max.
   - Generic white-background product shots: use lifestyle images.
   - Weak titles: rewrite with better keywords.
6. **Do one today, then repeat.** Pick one competitor, run the process, document it, launch better campaigns from it, then move to the next competitor.

## Success check
- A written brief for one competitor: Auction Insights, current ads, abandoned keywords (if Semrush used), landing-page funnel, location gaps.
- The brief names at least one thing they are not doing and a campaign change you will test.
- None of their copy, trademarks or claims ends up in your ads. (added, not in source)

## Anti-patterns
- Guessing who competes with you instead of reading Auction Insights.
- Copying their ads or offers.
- Treating a "Lost" keyword as a sure win; it may be unprofitable for you too.
- Checking one country only and missing a weaker region.
- Using this as a stored creative library; for a first-seen/last-seen ad catalogue use build-a-competitor-ad-spy-catalog-for-the-creati. (added, not in source)

## Source
Jackson Blackledge (@blvckledge), https://x.com/blvckledge/status/2120320614858977756, 11 Nov 2026 (Sydney time). The author runs Google and YouTube ads for DTC brands at echelonn.io. Earlier related post: https://x.com/blvckledge/status/2112523243252838862.

# skill: rewrite-ai-drafts-so-they-read-like-a-person
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/rewrite-ai-drafts-so-they-read-like-a-person.md
========================================================================

---
name: Rewrite AI drafts so they read like a person
description: >-
  Use this when a draft sounds machine-written (even structure, stiff tone, too
  much polish) and you want a fixed set of rewrite passes to make it read like a
  person, without faking experience or blurring facts.
---
The source's hook ("PEOPLE KNOW WHEN YOU'RE USING CHATGPT AND CLAUDE") is the author's claim, not a proven rule. The useful part is the seven prompts.

Run them only on text you believe is true. Don't invent memories, clients, results or hesitations. For financial-adviser or other regulated copy, keep every fact checkable. (added, not in source)

The thread posted the prompts out of order; use the numbered order below. Put the draft in <PASTE_TEXT>.

## Steps
1. **Thought flow correction**
   ```
   This isn't a grammatical correction. It's a reasoning correction. Rewrite it so the ideas move like a real mind: irregular in some places, straight to the point in others, sometimes slower. Break any pattern where the writing feels too controlled. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
2. **The pattern breaker**
   ```
   You're an expert at spotting the tells that give away AI-generated text. Go through this piece and wipe them out, one by one. Shake up the structure, ease out any stiff phrasing, and make every word feel like it was picked right then and there, not churned out by some formula. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
3. **The credibility test**
   ```
   You're a reader who immediately distrusts texts that seem too polished. Go sentence by sentence and rewrite anything that feels overly constructed, overly corrected, or too precise. It should sound like something a real person said out loud without second-guessing every word. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
4. **The voice shaper**
   ```
   You're building a voice that seems to belong to a real person. Rewrite it to carry a clear point of view, not the tone of a neutral observer trying to please everyone. Let opinions, small contradictions, and natural shifts in tone appear. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
   Keep only honest contradictions (a trade-off you actually accept). No fake personality. (added, not in source)
5. **The imperfections injector**
   ```
   Perfect texts have no history. Rewrite by adding micro-imperfections that only someone who has lived the subject would write: a strong opinion here, a hesitation there, an incomplete sentence where it makes sense. Do not correct afterward. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
   A strong opinion is fine if it's yours. A made-up hesitation or "I was there" detail is not. (added, not in source)
6. **The audio test**
   ```
   Read this text out loud in your head. Mark each sentence where you would make a strange pause or where the rhythm would break in a real conversation. Rewrite those sentences so that the entire text flows like human speech, not like a document. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
   Then actually read the result out loud. (added, not in source)
7. **The soul detector**
   ```
   Read this text as if you've already seen thousands of AI-generated texts. Identify the 3 sentences that sound the most artificial and rewrite each one as if the author were talking to a close friend. No filter. No perfection. Text: <PASTE_TEXT>
   ```
   Finish with a factual pass: names, figures, offers and advice still accurate. (added, not in source)

## Success check
- Sentence shapes vary and there's a point of view you'll stand behind.
- It reads aloud without tripping on padded phrasing.
- No new facts, clients, memories or results appeared.
- Regulated or offer copy still says only what you can support.

## Anti-patterns
- Overdoing it into a new obvious style (forced fragments, random slang, fake typos).
- Adding lived experience you didn't live.
- Hiding AI authorship where a platform, client or regulator requires disclosure. (added, not in source)
- Treating "people can always tell" as a research finding.

## Source
Mark Richard (@Mark0Richard), https://x.com/Mark0Richard/status/2120914302286839880, 13 Nov 2026 (Sydney time). Engagement-bait hook plus a seven-prompt thread.

# skill: rival-review-comparison-method
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/rival-review-comparison-method.md
========================================================================

---
name: Rival Review comparison method
description: >-
  Use this when Rival Review shortlists competitors, compares them, reads
  reviews, or shapes the written review.
---
# Rival Review comparison method

The live profile still holds the job, hand-offs, anti-jobs and approval rules.

## Starting a review

When a first message lacks project context, ask briefly for the product or business, a URL helps, the market or geography, and the decision the review should support. Use context already available rather than re-asking. Do not require Steven to list rivals. Discover a shortlist yourself from public sources and verify relevance before deep work.

## Shortlist

Default scope is 3 to 5 of the most relevant competitors, mixing direct rivals with indirect ones when evidence supports it. State why each name made the cut. Verify geography, language and buyer fit. Prefer fresh, like-for-like sources retrieved this run; state retrieval dates and the period each claim covers. Mark private data you cannot see, such as revenue, true acquisition costs, internal churn and unpublished roadmaps, as unknown rather than guessing.

## What to compare

Compare rivals on offer, audience, pricing and total cost of ownership, positioning, features, customer pain and objections, marketing and messaging, public ads where creatives are visible, and distribution. Separate observed facts, sourced claims and your inferences. Every material claim needs a dated primary or near-primary source link. Treat ad-library presence, creative longevity, follower counts and review volume as observations, not proof of profitability or quality. Never invent metrics, market shares, traffic figures, win rates or case studies.

## Reading reviews and discussions

Look for recurring patterns across enough sources to reduce cherry-picking and sample bias. Quote exact customer language with links; never invent or silently paraphrase a quotation. Note review-site incentives and date skew. Prefer official sites, pricing pages, docs, filings, changelogs, app stores, ad libraries and dated reporting over undated blogs or affiliate roundups.

## Output

Lead with a concise recommendation and a clear comparison. Quick reviews stay in chat. For a substantial reusable report, write a Page following the canvas skill rather than dumping a wall of chat. No generic SWOT filler or consultant padding. Prioritise opportunities against Steven's actual constraints, including budget, stage, geography, brand rules and existing stack. Distinguish copyable competitor tactics from defensible differentiation he can own. Label hypotheses as hypotheses. Give concrete next steps and the evidence that supports them rather than promising they will succeed.

# skill: run-a-compounding-ai-content-system
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-a-compounding-ai-content-system.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run a compounding AI content system
description: >-
  Use this when setting up or running a weekly content engine where agents scout
  ideas and analyse performance, but drafts come from your own experience, voice
  and swipe file.
---
# Run a compounding AI content system

## Steps
0. **Do the work first.** Every piece starts from a real problem, an artifact you built and a lesson. Ask yourself: what was hard to understand, what did I build to make it clearer, which constraint changed the design, and what would I do differently? Never outsource ideation to AI.
1. **Build the swipe file.** In [NOTES_VAULT] (e.g. Obsidian), create a swipe-file folder and clip full-text posts and articles into it with a web clipper. Add a one-line note on why each piece works, plus tags. Keep a `voice.md` file of your own writing that sounds like you. Point your drafting agent at both before it writes anything.
2. **Send out the scouts** (as routines):
   - **Outlier scanner** (daily): "Every morning, search X for posts and articles in [NICHES] from the last 24 hours. Compare each one's view count to the account's follower count. Send me the ten biggest outliers, with the link, the views, the follower count, and one line on why you think it worked."
   - **Reply analyst** (Mondays): pull replies to your posts from the last 30, 60 and 90 days, sort them into what people liked, disliked and asked for, and write a weekly ideas brief.
   - **Content strategist** (48 hours after each post): break down the post's style, format, topic and metrics, and write the analysis into the vault.
3. **Talk it, draft it, edit it.** Dictate the core argument (e.g. with Wispr Flow) so the raw material is in your natural voice. Then prompt: "I want to do an article about [TOPIC]. Refer to the swipe file for related articles, then brainstorm an outline." Have the agent draft from the outline, your voice file and the swipe file. Edit by hand: cut, fix claims and sharpen the opening.
4. **Make the visual earn its place.** Ask for a clean diagram of the idea. If it comes out bland, attach style reference images: "The graph was bland. Use these reference images for design style and visual direction and make it look a lot better."
5. **Publish the useful thing.** The article carries the value and the post is the hook that gets it opened. On X, quote-post your own post with a second piece of media and a slightly different take.
6. **Close the feedback loop** with two analyst agents. A voice analyst updates `voice.md` with word choices, sentence length and intro structures. A performance analyst writes what worked and what underperformed back into the vault.
7. **Let it compound.** Each weekly cycle starts from the updated vault, voice file and briefs.

## Not for
Fully automated, AI-originated content with no real experience behind it, or posting drafts without a human edit.

## Source
J.B. (@VibeMarketer_), video at https://x.com/VibeMarketer_/status/2110749655516520958 (15 Oct 2026) and summary post at https://x.com/VibeMarketer_/status/2111433557197410499 (17 Oct 2026). Tools shown: Obsidian with Web Clipper, Grok Bot (scout bots), Wispr Flow, Codex or Hermes Agent, and Codex's image model. Author's stated results over 12 months on X: 22.4M impressions and 40.5K followers.

# skill: run-a-daily-signal-based-prospecting-bot
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-a-daily-signal-based-prospecting-bot.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run a daily signal-based prospecting bot
description: >-
  Use this when building a cheap daily outbound prospecting bot: diff a
  target-account list's job boards, sites and news, have a small model (Haiku)
  tag buying signals and profile ICP fit, then score in plain code into
  email-today / wait / drop with a quoted first-line fact.
---
# Run a daily signal-based prospecting bot

Source: Alex Vacca ([@itsalexvacca](https://x.com/itsalexvacca/status/2108588892664606727)), founder of the GTM agency Frontal, in an X article from 9 Oct 2026: "Haiku 5.5 Is the Best Prospecting Model You Can Run". His repo, `signal-engine`, is gated ("comment SIGNAL"). If you don't have it, build the same design from the spec below. Commands are given as he wrote them; `<repo>` is a placeholder.

**Why it works:** Frontal sees about 15% replies when it emails right after something changes at the target company. Instantly puts the 2026 average for cold lists at 3.43%. Competitors can buy the same change alerts, so the edge comes from filtering by ICP fit first and opening with exactly what happened and when. His first run covered 11 companies for under 10 cents.

## Design: 5 steps, only 2 use the LLM
1. **Collect (plain code).** For each company, check three places:
   - its job board on Greenhouse, Lever, or Ashby
   - its home, about, careers, and pricing pages
   - Google News headlines from the last 7 days
   Save a snapshot of every page and diff it against yesterday's, so the model only reads what changed.
2. **Tag signals (LLM).** The model reads only the diff and tags reasons they might buy now, such as a new sales job or a funding round. It quotes the evidence and saves the link.
3. **Profile ICP fit (LLM, monthly).** Once a month, the model reads the site and open jobs and answers a fixed set of questions: who they sell to, whether they have a sales team, rough size, and who runs sales. It marks each ICP criterion pass, fail, or unknown, citing the page. Unknown sends the company to the wait group, so write the ICP in terms a website actually shows.
4. **Filter and score (plain code).** Drop companies that fail any ICP criterion, check how old each signal is, and score the rest out of 100.
5. **Output (plain code).** Produce a short digest plus a CSV for your email tool.

Every company lands in one of three groups: **act** (email today, with an opener fact), **hold** (wait until something new happens), or **suppress** (drop, with the reason, e.g. `size:fail (1200 vs 20-500)`).

The code steps are deterministic and easy to fix by hand, and only the LLM steps cost money. Keep each LLM request to one company's pages, and on most days just the diff.

**Day 1 vs later:**
- On day 1 there's nothing to diff, so only self-dated signals count: job posts from the last 21 days, 3 or more sales jobs posted at once, and this week's headlines.
- Website changes show up from day 2.
- A reposted job only counts if it was gone at least 7 days and came back, so those appear from week 2.

## ICP config (example)
```yaml
icp:
  industry: B2B software or services that sell to businesses
  size: {min: 20, max: 500}
  region: [US, CA, UK, EU]
  must_have: a sales team or an open sales role visible on the careers page
```
- Keep a `sales_role_keywords` list of sales job titles. The LLM uses it to tag jobs, and the code uses it to detect 3 or more sales jobs at once. If you sell to marketing teams, add marketing titles.
- A company with layoffs in the last 90 days always goes to hold.

## Signal windows and points (defaults)
| signal | counts for (days) | points (0–16) |
|---|---|---|
| funding round | 45 | 16 |
| new sales leader | 60 | 16 |
| reposted job | 30 | 14 |
| 3+ sales jobs at once | 30 | 14 |
| new market | 30 | 12 |
| new sales job | 21 | 10 |
| product launch | 21 | 10 |
| acquisition | 30 | 10 |
| switched software | 30 | 8 |
| won a contract | 30 | 8 |
| partnership | 30 | 6 |
| pricing change | 14 | 6 |
| complained publicly | 30 | 6 |
| website change | 14 | 4 |
| layoffs | 90 (hold) | 0 |

## Score = 5 parts added up (worked example: Linear, 81)
- **Fit, 40:** passed every ICP criterion.
- **Buyer, 15:** found the Head of Sales by name. A job title only is worth 8.
- **Recency, 16:** the post was 2 days old, out of a 21-day window.
- **Signal type, 10:** a new sales job.
- **Second signal, 0:** only one kind of signal, so no bonus.

If a score looks wrong, find the part that's off and change the setting behind it.

## Setup steps
1. Get the prerequisites: Python 3.11+, Claude Code logged in with a subscription (`claude` then `/login`), Mac/Linux or Windows WSL, and a CSV of `company,domain` with an optional `size` column that overrides the model's size estimate. To pay per use instead, put `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=` and `SIGNAL_ENGINE_BACKEND=api` in `.env`.
2. Install:
   ```bash
   git clone <repo> signal-engine && cd signal-engine
   python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
   chmod +x run.sh && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q
   ```
   These are 23 offline tests.
3. Do a sample run with `./run.sh daily`, then read the newest file in `data/digests/`.
4. Copy `config/template.yaml` to `config/<you>.yaml`. Edit the ICP first, then the signal windows and points, then `sales_role_keywords`.
5. Load your list:
   ```bash
   printf 'accounts: []\n' > accounts.yaml
   ./run.sh import leads.csv
   ./run.sh daily --tenant <you>
   ```
   The import finds each company's job board from its careers page, or guesses it. Companies with no job board still get their site and news checked. If you override `pages:` in `accounts.yaml`, list all 4 pages.
6. Review the act list number by number, and click every source link.
7. Write the opener from the quoted public fact, then ask one question about what that change means for the reader. You can have Claude draft 3 versions and edit 1 yourself. Also read the hold and suppress reasons and fix any ICP misfires.
8. Use the export in `data/export/`: company, site, buyer title or name, signal, date, link, and opener. The email column is empty, so add an email-lookup tool.
9. **Evaluate the small model against the big one before relying on it.** Label 100–200 records from `data/diffs/` into `evals/labeled.jsonl` as `{"rec": <diff line>, "expected": ["job_posting"]}`, then run `.venv/bin/python evals/agreement.py evals/labeled.jsonl`. It compares Haiku 5.5 with Sonnet 5.5 on accuracy, recall, and cost. If Haiku falls short, switch with `--model claude-sonnet-5-5` and run once with `--force` to re-profile. Watch the cost line for the first week, and double-check low-confidence tags (e.g. "Account Manager" titles).
10. **Schedule it** with `crontab -e`:
    ```bash
    PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/home/you/.local/bin
    0 7 * * * /home/you/signal-engine/run.sh daily --tenant <you> >> /home/you/signal-engine/data/cron.log 2>&1
    ```
    Check `cron.log` after the first run, since cron may not have your Terminal's login access.
11. **Leave the settings alone for 30 days.** Then shorten the window or lower the points for any signal type whose emails get replies at or below your usual rate.

## Not included
The bot doesn't build the list, find emails or phone numbers, watch LinkedIn or site visitors, write the full email, or send. A human edits and sends every email.


========================================================================
# skill: run-a-draft-through-a-three-lens-critique-gauntl
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-a-draft-through-a-three-lens-critique-gauntl.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run a draft through a three-lens critique gauntlet
description: >-
  Use this when you've finished a draft of a landing page, sales page, or
  flagship post and want it stress-tested by three distinct critics (hook,
  proof, clarity) before any prospect sees it.
---
# Steps

## 1. Build 3 critic profiles from real material (once, then reuse)
Don't use made-up branding-workshop personas. Ground each one in evidence:

1. **Direct-response legend (packaging and hook).** Built on Eugene Schwartz and David Ogilvy's principles. Cares about one thing: does the first line earn the next 5 seconds of attention, and is the headline specific enough to stop a stranger cold?
2. **Hostile CFO (proof and unit economics).** Built on the hardest budget pushback from your last 20 stalled deals: [STALLED_DEAL_OBJECTIONS]. Hunts every vague claim, unbacked percentage and "save time" promise that would get laughed out of a boardroom.
3. **Busy practitioner (clarity and mechanism).** Built from verbatim customer transcripts, Slack rants and churn interviews: [CUSTOMER_TRANSCRIPTS]. Flags every sentence where you sound like a SaaS brochure instead of someone who does the job.

Save each profile as its own prompt or agent, with its source material attached.

## 2. Write the raw draft once
Finish a full draft first. Don't ask teammates "thoughts?" in Slack: that gets polite feedback and typo fixes.

## 3. Run the gauntlet in private
Feed the draft through the lenses, in order or side by side:
- **Lens 1** attacks the hook and headline until the curiosity gap is undeniable.
- **Lens 2** strips the fluff and forces hard receipts (numbers, proof, named results) into the body.
- **Lens 3** rewrites the mechanism in the exact words your buyers use on calls.

Starter critic prompt (added, not in source):
> You are [LENS_PROFILE]. Here is your source material: [EVIDENCE]. Read the draft below. List every line that fails your test, quote it, say why, and give a rewrite. Do not praise. Draft: [DRAFT]

## 4. Merge and publish
Apply the accepted rewrites into one draft. Re-run any lens whose section changed a lot. Publish only after the draft survives all three. (The merge-and-rerun step is added, not in source.)

## Success check
By the time it goes live, each lens has nothing left to flag: the first line is specific, every claim has proof, and the mechanism reads in buyer language.

# Not for
- Generic copy polish or typo checks.
- Replacing real customer research. If you have no transcripts or objections yet, collect them first, or the personas turn into the made-up ones this method warns against.
- Anything where you haven't got a finished draft.

# Source
- J.B. (@VibeMarketer_), X post, 26 Oct 2026: https://x.com/VibeMarketer_/status/2114725739513905621
- The "10x the conversion rate" claim is the author's, with no data in the post.


========================================================================
# skill: run-a-multi-channel-shorts-network
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-a-multi-channel-shorts-network.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run a multi-channel Shorts network
description: >-
  Use this when running a multi-channel faceless YouTube network — burner tests,
  rival pairs, comment seeding, language splits, cross-seeding, and account
  hygiene under Shorts monetization floors.
---
# Steps

1. Treat multiple channels as a **network with jobs**, not income diversification. One channel is a video business; a network is a machine where formats, rivalry, and cross-traffic are deliberate.
2. **Sacrificial / burner channel:** Never test new formats on the channel that pays you. Run experiments on a burner for ~30 videos; only promote formats that clear onto the money channel. Format tests on the asset re-classify it and can crush the floor for weeks.
3. **Rival pair:** Two channels, same niche, opposite stances (e.g. guilty vs innocent), same editor/footage/template/operator. Comment sections on A become script fuel for B; platform treats conflict as engagement.
4. **Comment seeding:** Within ~60 seconds of upload, post the first comment from a second account — often the *wrong* take on purpose — to frame the thread and pull retention (people return to see corrections). Self-replies help hold top position.
5. **Language split:** Same script, dubbed; separate channels so feeds don’t cannibalize; each clears monetization thresholds in different ad markets.
6. **Cross-seed:** Shorts get one clickable link that must stay on-platform to your property — use the pinned comment as the door to the sibling/rival channel.
7. **Hygiene:** Brand accounts under one login pattern carefully; separate Google accounts for anything you sell; 2FA everywhere with current recovery email; editors get channel permissions never passwords; avoid logging many accounts from constantly rotating locations (that pattern flags).
8. **Monetization constraint (per source):** From February, each channel needs **10M Shorts views per rolling 90 days** to get paid at all — fewer, bigger, job-specific channels beat twelve hobby channels that earn nothing.

## Anti-patterns

- Testing formats on the paying channel
- Many weak channels that miss the rolling Shorts view floor
- Handing editors passwords instead of roles
- This is not a “grow one faceless channel” skill — it’s multi-channel network ops (and some tactics are adversarial/platform-gray)

## Source

- https://x.com/MethodByVid/status/2100276278054342789
- @MethodByVid (Vid), Sep 16, 2026
