# skill: run-a-music-release-promo-checklist
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-a-music-release-promo-checklist.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run a music release promo checklist
description: >-
  Use this when planning and running promotion for a single or EP release — an
  8-week phased checklist from distribution and rights setup through pre-saves,
  pitching, release-day activation, post-release follow-ups, value-first
  Reddit/Discord promo, and a T+4-week performance review.
---
# Steps

Run one copy of this checklist per release. Fill the header, set targets before you spend, and work phase by phase. Dates are relative to release day (T-0).

**Header**
- Release name:
- Release date:
- Current phase:

## Phase 1 — Operational setup and rights (T-8 to T-4 weeks)

**Distribution**
- [ ] Production and post-production finished
- [ ] Final master exported
- [ ] Final master submitted to distributor
- [ ] Release date scheduled about 8 weeks out (leaves room for editorial pitching)
- [ ] Metadata complete (titles, ISRC, credits, genre, explicit flag, artwork)
- [ ] Distributor review passed, then submit

**Rights and royalties**
- [ ] Registered with your performing-rights organisation (source used Buma Stemra, Netherlands)
- [ ] Registered with your neighbouring-rights / recording-rights body (source used Sena)
- [ ] Credits verified (writers, producers, featured artists, splits)

**Sync and licensing**
- [ ] Full version submitted to sync platforms
- [ ] Instrumental version submitted to sync platforms

**Digital infrastructure**
- [ ] Smart link created
- [ ] Linktree (or link-in-bio) updated
- [ ] Bandcamp, Audius, and SoundCloud uploads prepared (scheduled or ready)

**Audience conversion**
- [ ] Download gate created (source used Hypeddit) to trade a free download for follows or email
- [ ] Pre-save campaign prepared

**Targets and baselines (set now, review at T+4)**
- [ ] Week-1 streams target
- [ ] Spotify followers gained target
- [ ] Email subscribers gained target
- [ ] Discord members gained target
- [ ] Playlist placements target
- [ ] Revenue target
- [ ] Content pieces published target
- [ ] Ad budget per platform written down (Facebook/Instagram ads, Feature.fm, YouTube ads, Spotify Marquee/Showcase). No paid line runs without a budget.

## Phase 2 — Pre-release campaign (T-4 to T-1 weeks)

**Algorithm preparation**
- [ ] Shortlist the top 25 relevant curators, radio shows, and blogs (source used getheard.fm) and write them down
- [ ] Playlist pitch written
- [ ] Spotify for Artists editorial pitch submitted (must be before release day)
- [ ] Pre-save campaign launched

**Outreach**
- [ ] Premiere channels contacted
- [ ] Blogs contacted for a release-day feature
- [ ] Personalised emails sent to your fan list
- [ ] UGC (user-generated content) assets prepared: clips, sound, prompt for fans

**Narrative and positioning**
- [ ] Track story defined: how the track came about and how you made it
- [ ] Core emotion defined: the emotional reason you made the track
- [ ] Release caption written for SoundCloud, Audius, and similar
- [ ] Short release announcement written for message boards and communities

**Content**
- [ ] Track breakdown
- [ ] “Out now” video
- [ ] Emotional-story video
- [ ] Promo video sized for posting in groups
- [ ] Content concepts drafted (from your own reference doc or hook bank)
- [ ] All content rendered and ready
- [ ] Upload schedule set

## Phase 2.5 — Lead-time submissions (T-1 to T-0 weeks)

Everything a third party needs before release day:

- [ ] Radio submissions and radio pitching platforms
- [ ] Relevant YouTube channels pitched for a feature
- [ ] Blog feature submissions, with draft copy attached
- [ ] Track sent to promo pools
- [ ] Track sent to your DJ email list
- [ ] Industry outreach (managers, agencies) done

## Phase 3 — Release day (T-0)

**Own platforms (SoundCloud, Bandcamp, Audius)**
- [ ] Posted
- [ ] Monetisation switched on
- [ ] Native promotion on (paid only if budgeted)
- [ ] Music video posted
- [ ] Shorts posted

**Platform updates**
- [ ] Website updated
- [ ] Branding / banners updated
- [ ] Link-in-bio updated
- [ ] Every profile updated

**Announcement**
- [ ] Release announcement published
- [ ] Posts pinned on profiles

**Community activation**
- [ ] Fan email sent
- [ ] Discord announcement posted
- [ ] Facebook communities posted (follow each group’s rules)
- [ ] X post made
- [ ] Reddit posts made, value-first (see rules below)
- [ ] DMs sent to people who said they want to hear it
- [ ] Blog features live and shared

## Phase 4 — Post-release momentum (T-0 to T+2 weeks)

**Ongoing promo**
- [ ] SubmitHub follow-ups on anything not placed
- [ ] Groover follow-ups
- [ ] Repost-exchange campaign
- [ ] Feature.fm ads running (if budgeted)
- [ ] Facebook and Instagram ads running (budget approved)
- [ ] Independent curator outreach finished
- [ ] Reddit promo, value-first
- [ ] Other submission services you use (source listed “Lets Submit” and Triple Vision promo)
- [ ] Discord self-promo and ad channels
- [ ] Radio, YouTube channel, and blog submissions continue
- [ ] Spotify Marquee and Showcase live (if budgeted and eligible)
- [ ] Check your bookmarks for promo options you missed

**Algorithm support**
- [ ] Audience reminded to save the track
- [ ] Audience reminded to share the track

**Content waterfall**
- [ ] Studio breakdown video posted
- [ ] Emotional-story video posted
- [ ] UGC campaign started on all platforms
- [ ] Sample pack posted
- [ ] TikTok trend-format post

## Phase 5 — Community and long tail (T+2 to T+4 weeks)

**Extra promo**
- [ ] Spotify Discovery Mode (weigh the royalty trade-off)
- [ ] Influencer or creator outreach
- [ ] Instagram broadcast channel
- [ ] Instagram collab posts
- [ ] YouTube ads

**Community**
- [ ] Discord discussion thread
- [ ] Community engagement posts
- [ ] Audience feedback collected
- [ ] Remix competition, only if the release clearly took off
- [ ] Replies to fan comments

**Organic community outreach**
- [ ] Reddit engagement done value-first
- [ ] Discord engagement done in existing threads before posting your own
- [ ] At least some genuine contributions made before each promo post

## Value-first Reddit and Discord rules

1. Read each subreddit’s or server’s self-promo rules before posting. Many have a ratio rule or a dedicated promo thread.
2. Contribute before you promote: answer questions in threads, share a free sample pack, post behind-the-scenes or production tips.
3. Post the track where it fits the community, with context (story, how it was made), not a bare link.
4. Use designated self-promo threads and ad channels where they exist.
5. Reply to every comment on your posts.
6. Do not spam the same post across many communities at once.

## Release performance review (T+4 weeks)

Record actuals next to the Phase 1 targets:

- Streams:
- Spotify followers gained:
- Email subscribers gained:
- Discord members gained:
- Playlist placements:
- Content pieces published:
- Revenue generated:
- Most successful content:
- Biggest lesson learned:
- What to improve next release:

**Long-term review**
- [ ] Lessons documented
- [ ] Performance reviewed against targets
- [ ] Changes noted in the next release’s copy of this checklist

## Agent notes

- An agent can draft pitches, captions, announcement posts, fan emails, and the curator shortlist, and track the checklist state. It must not post to communities, send emails or DMs, submit paid campaigns, or spend money without the artist’s explicit go-ahead per item.
- Platform names in brackets are the source’s picks. Swap in equivalents for your country or genre.

## Success check

- Release scheduled about 8 weeks out, with editorial pitch in before T-0.
- Rights and credits registered before release.
- Targets and ad budgets written before any spend.
- Every Reddit/Discord promo preceded by real contributions in that community.
- T+4 review filled in and fed into the next release.

## Source

- “Music promo checklist for Reddit” (Release & Promotion Checklist, actionable format), a `.docx` Steven shared via Dropbox on 8 Oct 2026. Dutch notes in the original translated to English; Netherlands rights bodies kept as examples.

# skill: run-a-performance-based-ugc-creator-program
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-a-performance-based-ugc-creator-program.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run a performance-based UGC creator program
description: >-
  Use this when building or scaling a paid-ads UGC creator program on a
  performance model (pay % of ad spend or GMV plus a smart retainer): recruit a
  few intent-based creators, build culture, scale 5→10→20→40, add referrals, and
  avoid Meta's similarity clustering.
---
# Run a performance-based UGC creator program

Source: Hector Serrano ([@hectorserrranoo](https://x.com/hectorserrranoo/status/2108260769603486100)), marketing hire #2 at Wispr Flow, 8 Oct 2026. It's a 15-minute video: "i built @WisprFlow's paid ads program — here's how i'd rebuild it in 30 days". In practice the video covers the creator program only. It does not cover campaign structure, bidding, targeting, or tracking, so pair this with [bulk-launch-meta-ads-from-a-template-ad](sand-workflow:bulk-launch-meta-ads-from-a-template-ad) and [warehouse-meta-ads-api-for-mutations-only](sand-workflow:warehouse-meta-ads-api-for-mutations-only).

Wispr Flow's benchmark is 500–700 net-new UGC ads launched every month.

## 1. Platform and performance model
- Stop paying thousands upfront for creatives that might not convert. Pay for performance instead.
- The loop: a creator joins your group, makes a video, you launch it as an ad, and you pay them a share of what it drives.
- Hector runs this on a creator marketplace called Trybe, which he describes as "TikTok Shop for every platform" (Meta, TikTok, AppLovin). Any equivalent tool, or a spreadsheet plus ad-ID tracking, works too.

## 2. Payment
- E-commerce brands pay a % of the GMV the ad drives.
- SaaS and info products pay a % of the ad spend behind the creator's videos, because their conversion cycles are long. Wispr pays 7% of ad spend.
- **Smart retainer:** this is a guaranteed monthly minimum for hitting a video quota, so new creators without performance history stay motivated. Wispr's version is 25 videos for $1,000 a month.
  - If commissions fall below the retainer, you top them up. For example, $500 earned plus a $500 top-up.
  - If commissions beat the retainer, you pay nothing extra. For example, they earn $3,000 and you add $0.

## 3. Recruit a few intent-based creators, not hundreds
- Don't hire hundreds of mercenary creators making identical talking-head videos. Meta clusters near-duplicate ads (roughly 60%+ similar) and suppresses their reach.
- Start with 4–5 creators chosen to fill gaps in your ad library: new ICPs (your ideal customer profiles), new formats, and new locations or languages.
- Source them off-platform at first, since you'll have no reviews yet. Use connections and creator groups.
- Instagram keyword search also works. Search terms like "UGC", "creator", "tech", and "SaaS", find one creator who meets your bar, then mine their followers, likes, and commenters for similar peers.
- Send 100–200 DMs over a few days to form the first group.

## 4. Culture: treat creators like an in-house sales team
- Transactional, box-checking relationships lead to churn and to your best creators getting poached.
- Offer 1:1 strategy calls. Wispr uses Calendly links to Hector.
- Run a weekly group call. Wispr's is on Thursdays with the marketer and the media buyer, covering ad-account patterns, new ICPs, and experiments.
- Run giveaways and bonuses, such as cash, cameras, mics, and Meta glasses.
- Hold in-person retreats for top creators. Wispr is flying its top 6 to the SF office for a week.

## 5. Scale deliberately
- Grow in steps of 5, then 10, 20, and 40, keeping the culture intact at each step. Wispr went from 5 to 50 active creators in about 4 months.
- At 40–60 creators, coast. From there, only add top-tier people to fill specific gaps. You rarely need more than 60.
- **Referral bonus:** pay an existing creator (Wispr pays $100) for bringing in a peer at or above their own level. Vet each referral's IG or portfolio and take no beginners.
- Keep the bar high. Wispr got about 7,000 marketplace applications and accepted only 5–7.

## 6. Fight creative stagnation
- Burnt-out creators copy the leaderboard's top formats. Meta then clusters those copies under the original and suppresses them.
- Push creators who are in a rut toward genuinely new concepts. The leaderboard leaders win by experimenting, not by copying.
- Use the weekly call to assign new angles, ICPs, and formats.

## Checklist
- [ ] Pick a platform or tracking method that attributes spend or GMV to each creator's ads
- [ ] Set the commission % and the smart retainer (quota and minimum)
- [ ] Audit the ad library for gaps, then recruit 4–5 creators to fill them (100–200 DMs)
- [ ] Set up the Calendly 1:1 link, the weekly call, and a bonus budget
- [ ] Scale 5, 10, 20, 40, then cap around 60, with a referral bonus and vetting
- [ ] Review monthly for near-duplicate creatives and push new formats


========================================================================
# skill: run-abm-paid-media-from-claude-code-ads-engineer
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-abm-paid-media-from-claude-code-ads-engineer.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run ABM paid media from Claude Code (Ads Engineering)
description: >-
  Use this when one person runs B2B paid media and ABM across LinkedIn, Meta and
  Google from Claude Code: a tiered account list, exclusions and identifiers, 3
  agents plus reporting skills, 1:1 LinkedIn ads with a value page per account,
  ads-plus-outbound gating, an approval gate, and a 30-day plan.
---
# Run ABM paid media from Claude Code (Ads Engineering)

Sources: Alex Vacca ([@itsalexvacca](https://x.com/itsalexvacca/status/2109995654949077324), 13 Oct 2026) on the 3-layer ABM stack, and his article [Ads Engineering: The Complete Guide to Running Paid Media From Claude Code](https://x.com/itsalexvacca/status/2107511355062546530) (6 Oct 2026), describing how Ivan Falco runs paid media at Frontal.

**Results they report:**
- $33K of ads produced $887K of pipeline, aimed at 61 accounts with 3 ads each.
- One person runs more than $200K a month in spend; it used to take a team of 6.
- Ads plus outbound returned $51 of pipeline per $1, measured across the combined system.

Ivan's free skill pack is at frontal.so/resources/12-claude-code-skills-for-ad-management. Some of the article's tables (the scoring weights and tier definitions) weren't readable, so tune those yourself.

**Core rule:** Claude Code does the work, and a person approves every dollar. A person also owns three calls: the offer, the positioning, and which accounts get the money.

## The 3-layer ABM stack (build in this order)
1. **Scope the total addressable market (TAM) and pick targets.**
   - Firmographic match: Clay. Lookalikes of paying customers: Ocean.io. Research and ranking: Clay and Claude.
   - Verified emails and mobiles: Prospeo. Ad audiences from contacts: ContactLevel or Primer.
   - Fit isn't timing. A perfect fit with no signals waits; an account with 8 signals at once goes first.
2. **Give every account its own campaign.**
   - Person-level ads: Influ2. Company-level ads: LinkedIn and Meta.
   - A landing page per account: Mutiny, or Claude plus Vercel/Railway. Personal video: Sendspark.
   - Email: Instantly. Email plus LinkedIn DMs: lemlist. Calls: Aircall or Orum.
   - Each account's page gives something useful: a GTM report, a content audit, or feedback on its ads.
3. **Watch attention and move the budget there.**
   - Ad engagement: Fibbler, ZenABM, Vector. Site visits: Vector, RB2B. Product use: PostHog, Amplitude.
   - LinkedIn engagement: Apify. Pipeline attribution: HockeyStack, Factors.ai.
   - Skip this layer and your ads keep hitting the day-one list.

The platforms now handle bidding, placement, and creative delivery. Two things stay with you: **who is in the target market** (your closed-won data) and **what happened after the click** (your CRM).

## Folder setup
Install Claude Code and make an `ads/` folder containing `data/`, `data/crm/`, `data/exports/raw/`, `.claude/agents/`, `.claude/skills/`, `scripts/`, `scripts/write/`, `pages/`, `creative/`, and `brand/`. Apply for API access on day one, because LinkedIn reviews every request and Google needs brand verification.

## Layer 1: the target account list
1. **Export from the CRM into `data/crm/`:**
   - `closed_lost.csv`, `stalled_deals.csv`, and `old_mqls.csv` become the list.
   - `closed_won.csv` (with a one-line `use_case` per customer) and `closed_won_contacts.csv` define fit and seed lookalikes.
   - `open_opps.csv` and `competitors.csv` go in the exclusion list.
   Cap the list at 500–3,000 accounts, and give every account a written reason to be there. If you're short, top up with Clay lookalikes marked source `net-new`.
2. **Score fit and timing as two separate numbers.**
   - Fit covers size, industry, geography, stack, revenue model, buying committee, and resemblance to closed-won.
   - Timing covers hiring, funding, a new leader, a stack change, or key-page visits.
   - Pull signals with Clay or PredictLeads into `data/signals.csv` (columns: domain, signal, date). Frontal keeps a library of 54 triggers.
   - Prompt: *"Score every row in data/tal.csv with the rules in data/scoring.md. Count only signals from the last 30 days. Add the columns fit, signals, signal_list, tier, and use_case (copy the use_case of the most similar closed-won customer). Show me the count per tier before saving."*
   - Signal count alone never makes Tier 1. Strong fit with no signal stays in an always-on audience.
3. **Tiers decide the effort.** Each tier must change the budget, the audience, the page, or the creative.
4. **Contacts:** pull the buying-committee titles at Tier 1–3 accounts into `data/contacts.csv` (name, title, company, domain, work email, LinkedIn URL). Do the same for the exclusions into `exclude_contacts.csv`.
5. **Keep target contacts and closed-won contacts in separate lists.** On Meta, build a separate 1% lookalike from each; Meta needs at least 100 people per seed. Meta's Advantage+ settings treat lookalikes as a suggestion, so put the exclusions under Audience Controls, where they're a hard limit.
6. **Buy identifiers before uploading to Meta.** Meta matches on personal emails and phone numbers, so run contacts through Prospeo or FullEnrich, and count that cost as part of the media budget. Check consent and lawful basis with privacy first. **Never send bought data to Google**, because Customer Match only allows data you collected. On LinkedIn, use its template with the headers unchanged; lists need 300+ rows, and 1,000+ companies is recommended.
7. **Build the exclusion audience first.** It covers customers, open opportunities, competitors, and disqualified accounts. Attach it to every prospecting campaign and keep it re-syncing.
8. **Sync automatically.** Clay Ads re-syncs to LinkedIn, Meta, and Google every 3 days. Build its table from the CRM integration, not a CSV, so it stays current. Check match rates after 48 hours. Google Customer Match needs 90 days of account history and more than $50K lifetime spend.
9. **Wire one live signal: site visits.**
   - Vector or RB2B (US-focused) identifies the company and sends it to Clay by webhook.
   - Clay qualifies it against the account list and CRM, then stages 6–8 buying-committee contacts.
   - You approve the staged accounts every Monday, and they go into one pooled LinkedIn retargeting audience at 12+ impressions per person. Seed that pool with the Tier 1–2 committees so it starts above LinkedIn's 300-member minimum.

LinkedIn limits to plan around: matching a list takes up to 48 hours, retargeting only counts visits made after the audience exists, and ad review takes under 24 hours. Keep the target list and retargeting audiences live at all times.

## Agents: 3 in `.claude/agents/`
- **ads-reporting:** audits, pacing, fatigue, and reports. It never changes anything. Every report answers, in order:
  1. Where did the money go?
  2. Who saw the ads?
  3. What changed in the auction?
  4. Which creative lost attention?
  5. What reached pipeline?
  It compares against the previous window of the same length and checks data freshness first.
- **ads-campaign-manager:** builds, targeting, bids, budgets, and optimization.
- **ads-creative:** research, concepts, copy, and designs, working from the brand rules in `brand/`.

The loop: reporting finds the issue, a person decides, campaign-manager makes the change, and creative hands new ads to campaign-manager. Restart Claude Code after adding agents or skills.

## Skills: 12, built boring-first
- **Build first:** spend-tracker (where the money moved) and performance-auditor (what changed around it), starting with 20% change lines and a 100 spend floor, tuned after 2 weeks.
- **Next:** creative-fatigue-analyzer plus `fatigue_rules.json` set to `{"ctr_drop":0.30,"max_weekly_frequency":2.0,"min_weekly_impressions":1000}`, run with `scripts/fatigue_check.py`. Drop the impression floor to 200 for 1:1 ad sets. A LinkedIn flag usually means the audience ran out of people; a Meta flag means the ad lost attention and needs a new angle.
- **The rest:**
  - Diagnose: search-terms, keyword-analyzer.
  - Monitor: fatigue-monitor.
  - Execute: bid-optimizer, bulk-editor, two audience-builders, creative-builder, negative-keywords.
- **Data feed:** export at least 4 complete weeks of ad-level data per platform into `data/exports/raw/` and merge it into one file that every skill reads.
- **Platform roles:**
  - LinkedIn suits known accounts.
  - Meta brings B2B volume from your own data and needs 10–20 new ads every 1–2 weeks.
  - Google captures existing demand, so review search terms weekly and add negatives.
- **Honesty checks on every alert:** data freshness (newest row date), missing fields or days, and recent campaign changes that could explain the movement.
- **Audience decay** looks good on the dashboard (CTR up, CPL down) while the leads get worse. Alert on it against qualified pipeline from the CRM.

## LinkedIn 1:1 ABM build
1. **Qualify accounts.** Only accounts with 300+ members after the cuts get their own ad set, which in practice means enterprise. Smaller accounts go into 1:few groups by shared problem or vertical: a company list if the group is 300+, otherwise added by name. LinkedIn's "campaign" is now the old campaign group, and its "ad set" is the old campaign; the API still uses the old names.
2. **Map company names to LinkedIn company page IDs** through the API, and fix subsidiaries by hand.
3. **Narrow to the buying committee** in `data/buying_committee.md`: locations, then either seniority (CXO, VP, Director) with functions (Sales, Marketing), or job titles. You can't use both functions and titles. Target 300–1,000 members. Turn off Audience Expansion and LinkedIn Audience Network, and use no interest targeting.
4. **Make a value page per account.** Research it with ads-creative into `pages/<acct>/research.md`, using only sourced facts. `pages/TEMPLATE.md` sets the structure: a headline naming the company, the useful thing you made for it, one proof point from a similar customer, and one CTA. Include the LinkedIn Insight Tag and deploy with `npm i -g vercel && vercel login`.
5. **Make 3 ads per account,** each naming the company and speaking to the use case of similar customers. Use one Figma template with a company-name text layer, exported as `creative/<acct>/ad1-3.png`.
6. **Budget.** The minimum is $10 a day per ad set. The monthly floor is ad sets × daily budget × 30, so 50 accounts cost about $15K a month. Set a campaign total budget, and **create everything paused** in one campaign. Review it in one pass, then launch with a single command after your yes.
7. **Send results back.** Post CRM stages through LinkedIn's Conversions API: MQL and SQL as qualified-lead conversions, won deals as PURCHASE, within 90 days.

**Pre-launch checklist:**
- [ ] Every account is still 300+ after the cuts
- [ ] Company IDs are verified, with subsidiaries checked
- [ ] Audiences are 300–1,000
- [ ] Audience Expansion and Audience Network are off, with no interest targeting
- [ ] Exclusions are attached
- [ ] Each account has 3 ads naming it
- [ ] Every page has been read, uses only sourced facts, is live with the Insight Tag, and is linked from the ads
- [ ] The budget floor fits, with a campaign total set
- [ ] Everything is paused

## Ads plus outbound on one list
1. Give every CRM account four fields: owner, tier, stage, and next action. Keep signals in the account history. A signal that changes nothing is just noise.
2. Write one rule per signal (what it triggers).
3. **Gate outbound until the account has seen your ads.** An account enters the ad audience the week its signal fires; outbound becomes eligible once impressions pass the threshold set in CLAUDE.md. Fibbler syncs company-level LinkedIn ad views into the CRM.
4. **Measure against a control.** Either hold out half of comparable accounts (half get ads before outbound, half get cold outbound) and compare reply, meeting, pipeline, and revenue; or flag accounts exposed to ads and split outbound results by that flag. Report the result as a lift on outbound, not on last touch.

## Connect, guardrail, run
- **LinkedIn:** a Developer Portal app with Advertising API access (scopes `r_ads`, `rw_ads`, `r_ads_reporting`; the Development tier allows edits on 5 accounts). Matched Audiences and the Conversions API need separate requests.
- **Meta:** the official ads MCP server (beta), which creates campaigns paused. Accounts you don't own need Advanced Access plus Business Verification.
- **Google:** the official MCP server is read-only; make changes through the Google Ads API under a Cloud project (no developer tokens since 9 Sep 2026). Apply for Explorer access or higher.
- **CRM:** the HubSpot MCP, or re-export every Monday.
- **CLAUDE.md:** the accounts, the naming rule, money rules, daily budgets, and the warm-up threshold.
- **Approval gate in `.claude/settings.json`:**
  ```json
  {"permissions":{"allow":["Bash(python3 scripts/fatigue_check.py *)","mcp__google-ads"],"ask":["mcp__meta-ads","Bash(python3 scripts/write/*)"]}}
  ```
  Every script that writes to an ad account lives in `scripts/write/`, so this one rule covers them. "Ask" rules survive "don't ask again".
- **Weekly rhythm:** 3 days changing where the money goes, 2 days reading what it did.

## First 30 days
1. **Week 1:** build spend-tracker and performance-auditor, sync the CRM, and set up the exclusion list on every platform, confirming it re-syncs. No new spend.
2. **Week 2:** build the two contact lists, buy identifiers, upload, and read the match rates. The match rate is your ceiling.
3. **Week 3:** launch one prospecting campaign, either lookalikes from closed-won, a named-list segment, or signal-based. Optimize for leads, run 10+ creatives, split the landing page 50/50, and write the daily budget into CLAUDE.md.
4. **Week 4:** wire buying-committee retargeting from site visits and the return path. Send MQL, SQL, and won stages back through the LinkedIn and Meta Conversions APIs. Meta's Conversion Leads optimization needs 200+ leads a month, daily uploads, and the stage reached within 28 days. Move the optimization goal from leads to MQL to SQL as volume allows.

Related: [bulk-launch-meta-ads-from-a-template-ad](sand-workflow:bulk-launch-meta-ads-from-a-template-ad), [warehouse-meta-ads-api-for-mutations-only](sand-workflow:warehouse-meta-ads-api-for-mutations-only), [run-a-daily-signal-based-prospecting-bot](sand-workflow:run-a-daily-signal-based-prospecting-bot).

# skill: run-gtm-research-as-a-three-hour-sparring-sessio
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-gtm-research-as-a-three-hour-sparring-sessio.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run GTM research as a three-hour sparring session
description: >-
  Use this when you need a first go-to-market hypothesis from raw competitor,
  earnings, review and forum material, and you want an LLM as a sparring partner
  rather than a summariser.
---
# Goal
Turn a pile of primary material into a GTM hypothesis you can take to real buyers, in about three hours instead of weeks of unfocused research.

# Inputs
- 25–40 competitor websites, fully scraped: pricing pages, case studies and docs
- The last few earnings calls from the 3–5 biggest incumbents
- 100+ customer reviews (G2, Capterra, Trustpilot, app stores)
- Every Reddit or forum thread where people vent about the category
- An LLM you can iterate with (the post uses Claude)

# Steps
1. Do not start by typing "research the market for X". Feed the model the raw material above first.
2. Ask questions that force it to think, not summarise:

```
What do the winners in this market know that their customers would never admit?
```

```
List the beliefs this whole industry takes for granted. For each one, what would need to happen for it to be false?
```

3. In about 20 minutes you should see where everyone agrees, where everyone is blind, and which customer pains nobody is building for.
4. Pick your best angle and tell the model to tear it apart:

```
Steelman this thesis like a top-tier VC would. Then show me exactly where it fails.
```

5. Do a few rounds of that. After about three hours you want a first GTM hypothesis. Treat the model as a sparring partner that doesn't get tired or defensive when it's wrong.
6. It is still a hypothesis. The real work starts when you talk to actual buyers.
7. Follow scraping terms, copyright and site rate limits when collecting material. Don't feed scraped personal data into a public model. (added, not in source)

# Success check
- The raw corpus exists (sites, earnings, reviews, vent threads), not just a chat summary.
- You have a written hypothesis plus the strongest objections from the steelman rounds.
- You have a list of real buyers to test it with.

# Failure modes
- The "taught at Y Combinator" and "4 weeks into 3 hours" claims are the author's. Unverified.
- The model can invent pains that are not in the corpus. Every claim should point back to a page, call, review or thread you fed it. (added, not in source)
- Stopping at the hypothesis and never talking to buyers.

# Anti-patterns
- A one-shot "research this market" prompt with no source pile.
- Publishing or pitching the hypothesis as fact.
- Treating the closing Gojiberry mention (the author's product for finding people to test with) as a required step.

# Source
Guillaume Bardet (@GuillaumeBardet), https://x.com/GuillaumeBardet/status/2118657239217041552, 2026-11-06. The post promotes Gojiberry at the end.

# skill: run-seo-from-claude-code-with-two-api-keys
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-seo-from-claude-code-with-two-api-keys.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run SEO from Claude Code with two API keys
description: >-
  Use this when a SaaS or service business wants keyword research, a content
  calendar, per-vertical landing pages and a competitor link-building list from
  Claude Code, using a Keywords Everywhere key and a DataForSEO key.
---
# Goal
Replace an agency SEO retainer with one agent session driven by two API keys: keyword universe, competitor gaps, content calendar, per-vertical pages, link targets.

# Inputs
- [KEYWORDS_EVERYWHERE_API_KEY] and [DATAFORSEO_API_KEY], stored in a `.env` file the agent reads (never pasted into chat or committed).
- [SEED_KEYWORDS] and [YOUR_DOMAIN]
- [COMPETITOR_DOMAINS]: three or more
- [VERTICALS]: the industries you serve (the demo used 20)

# Steps
1. Put both keys in `.env`. Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. (added, not in source)
2. Keyword universe. Use Keywords Everywhere to pull related keywords and "people also search for" for each seed. Dedupe and save to a file with volume. The demo shows about 4,800 keywords.
3. Gap analysis. Send the keywords to the DataForSEO SERP API. For each one record who ranks (your domain plus [COMPETITOR_DOMAINS]) and flag keywords where no competitor ranks well. Those are the gaps. [Check DataForSEO docs for exact endpoints and per-call cost first.]
4. Content calendar. Cluster the gap keywords by intent or page type (pricing, "best for", vs, alternatives, integrations, templates, how-to, FAQ and so on). Lay them out as a week-by-week plan, one page per working day.
5. Vertical pages. For each of [VERTICALS], find long-tail keywords, then draft one unique page per vertical with structured data (schema) included. Each page needs real vertical-specific content, not a swapped industry name. (added, not in source)
6. Link building. Use DataForSEO's domain intersection to list every domain linking to two or more competitors but not to you. Rank by how many competitors each links to (the demo shows 3/3 and 2/3).
7. Review gate. Show the keyword file, calendar, page drafts and link list for human review before publishing anything or contacting any site. (added, not in source)

# Success check
- A saved keyword file, gap list, calendar, page drafts and ranked link list exist.
- Gap keywords really show no strong competitor in the SERP data.

# Failure modes
- API costs: DataForSEO charges per call. Check pricing and cap the batch size before step 3. (added, not in source)
- Thin templated vertical pages risk being treated as low-quality or duplicate content. (added, not in source)
- Search volume and SERP data are snapshots. Re-pull on a schedule.

# Not for
- Publishing pages or sending link-building outreach without review.
- Sites with no competitors to compare, or work that needs a GSC-first approach (see the striking-distance skill).
- Treating the post's "agency retainer in 2 API keys" as a verified result. It's the author's claim.

# Source
Cody Schneider (@codyschneider), https://x.com/codyschneider/status/2116274004684136742, 2026-10-30. Post promotes Graphed (the author's product); the method itself uses Keywords Everywhere and DataForSEO. The attached video is a motion-graphic, not a screen recording.

# skill: run-simple-cbo-meta-ads-and-test-messages-cheap
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-simple-cbo-meta-ads-and-test-messages-cheap.md
========================================================================

---
name: Run simple CBO Meta ads and test messages cheap
description: >-
  Use this when an ecommerce or lead-gen advertiser wants a simple Meta campaign
  structure, cheap message tests as native ads, then rebuilds of winners as
  richer formats, plus new-country duplicates and buyer groups mined from
  reviews.
---
# Goal
Keep Meta account structure simple so most of the work goes into creative. Test new messages in the cheapest format first, then rebuild only the messages that spend.

# Inputs
- <AD_ACCOUNT> with permission to create campaigns
- <PRODUCT> and its <PRIMARY_COUNTRY>
- Winning and losing native-ad copy, if any exist
- Customer reviews for <PRODUCT>
- <EXTRA_COUNTRIES> to try after a winner exists

# Steps
1. Build one campaign-budget-optimisation (CBO) campaign per product, and one country per campaign.
2. Inside each campaign, make one ad set per ad idea with three creatives: the same video with a different first 3 seconds on each. Use one primary text and one headline. Don't use a 3:2:2 structure. The author says this isn't the most optimised setup on paper; it exists to keep the focus on creative.
3. Scale the campaign budget about 20% up or down. If cost per acquisition (CPA) is off target, rarely scale down; test new creative instead. The author says simple CBO has kept beating bid caps and cost caps (unverified agency claim).
4. When a product already spends well in one or two countries, duplicate the winning ads into new CBO campaigns for <EXTRA_COUNTRIES>. Change nothing else first. Author's example: about $30k/week in the USA and Australia added about $17k/week in the UK and Canada at a lower CPA (unverified).
5. Produce in the formats the author says are spending now:
   - Native ads: long story posts or organic-looking photos.
   - Animations: Pixar-style dialogue or wireframes.
   - AI UGC.
   - Yapper ads: get-ready-with-me or car story-time with the product woven in. Yapper ads are not UGC; writing them the same way makes a bad one.
6. Write native ads for the buyer's actual awareness stage: problem-aware story for a problem-aware market, solution-aware story for a solution-aware one. Natives are not only for unaware markets.
7. Before writing new natives, give Claude (or your coding agent) both winning and losing native ads so it learns the difference.
8. Test every new message as a native ad first, since it's the cheapest to produce. If it spends, rebuild the same message as an animation and as an AI UGC video. The author prices a 10-minute animation at about $100–$200 in credits, so those formats only get proven messages.
9. Read customer reviews and list buyer groups you've never made an ad for. Build ads for them. The author says one unused buyer group unlocked another $100k/month in profitable spend (unverified).
10. Review spend, CPA and which messages earned rebuilds before raising budgets or adding countries. (added, not in source)

# Success check
- Each product has one CBO campaign per country, one ad set per idea, and three first-3-second variants.
- New messages were tested as natives before any expensive rebuild.
- A review-mined buyer group has at least one test ad.
- Country duplicates started from unchanged winning ads.

# Failure modes
- Spend, CPA and "$100k/month" figures are the author's agency results across 50+ accounts in one month (about 70% ecommerce, 30% lead gen). Unverified.
- Creative that works in one country can fail after a straight duplicate. Watch CPA before scaling the new country. (added, not in source)
- Natives that ignore awareness stage waste cheap tests.

# Anti-patterns
- Spending most of the week on account structure instead of creative.
- Rebuilding unproven messages as animations or AI UGC.
- Calling yapper ads UGC and writing them the same way.
- Ignoring platform ad policies or making deceptive claims. (added, not in source)
- Treating the closing agency pitch (DM "SCALE") as part of the method.

# Source
Nick Theriot (@nicktheriot_), thread https://x.com/nicktheriot_/status/2119415833713930372 and https://x.com/nicktheriot_/status/2119415839615275417, 2026-11-08. Agency results are the author's and unverified.

# skill: run-tiered-outbound-across-cold-email-linkedin-d
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/run-tiered-outbound-across-cold-email-linkedin-d.md
========================================================================

---
name: 'Run tiered outbound across cold email, LinkedIn DMs and cold calls'
description: >-
  Use this when you're setting up B2B outbound that needs to book meetings
  across email, LinkedIn and phone, and want one rule (account tier) that
  decides which channels each account gets, plus a setup playbook per channel.
---
# Steps

## 0. Tier your accounts first
Put a tier in its own column next to every account. Every channel reads it.
- **Tier 1:** strong fit with an active signal (new hire, funding round, from the last few weeks).
- **Tier 2:** strong fit, no signal yet.
- **Tier 3:** adjacent fit.
"Strong fit" = matches your best customers on industry, company size and buyer title. "Adjacent" = matches on some.

| Tier | Gets | Message |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Call + LinkedIn + email | 1 custom message per account |
| 2 | LinkedIn + email | Template with 1 variable swapped |
| 3 | Email only | High-volume sequences |

Never push a Tier 1 account into a high-volume email sequence.

## 1. Cold email (volume engine): 20 to 25 sends a day per warmed inbox
1. **List:** in [LIST_TOOL, e.g. Clay] use Find companies (best customers' industry and size), then Find people (buyer titles), then a work-email waterfall ([EMAIL_FINDER, e.g. Prospeo] first).
2. **Sending domains:** never send cold email from your main domain. Buy look-alike domains (e.g. get[yourcompany].com), add each to your mail provider, create 3 inboxes per domain.
3. **DNS on every domain:** one SPF, one DKIM, one DMARC record (merge duplicates). Example from the source (Google Workspace):
```
TXT @                  v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all
TXT google._domainkey  v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=...   (key generated in Google Admin: Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Authenticate email)
TXT _dmarc             v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@get[yourcompany].com
```
4. **Warm up** 2 to 4 weeks before the first send in [SENDER_TOOL, e.g. Instantly or lemlist] (Instantly's minimum is 2 weeks). Leave warm-up on after launch.
5. **Signals:** add new-hire and news/funding signals to the account list. A strong-fit account with a fresh signal moves to Tier 1 that week, and email 1 opens on that signal.
6. **3-email sequence about the situation behind the signal** (email 1 under 80 words, one question at the end). Example for a company that just hired a head of sales:
> EMAIL 1 (day 1) Subject: [first name]'s first quarter
> [First name], a new sales leader's first quarter usually comes with a pipeline target. We help [company type] with [the problem you solve]. Want me to send the 1-page plan we'd run for [company]?
>
> EMAIL 2 (day 4) Subject: re: [first name]'s first quarter
> [First name], 1 thing we see at [company type] in the first 90 days: [1 specific pattern]. [Customer] had the same setup and [1 short result]. Worth a look?
>
> EMAIL 3 (day 9) Subject: re: [first name]'s first quarter
> Last note from me, [first name]. The 1-page plan for [company] is ready whenever you'd like it. Just reply "send it".
- Tier 1: rewrite email 1 by hand per account, in its own low-volume campaign. Tier 2: swap the 1 line about their company. Tier 3: swap the signal line for 1 line about the problem you solve, send at volume.
7. **Ramp** a few sends a day up to 20 to 25 per inbox (Instantly recommends max 30). Volume comes from more inboxes: about 20 inboxes on 7 domains for 500 a day.
8. **A yes** is a reply asking for times. Answer within the hour:
> Great, [first name]. Does [DAY_1 TIME] or [DAY_2 TIME] ([TIMEZONE]) work? Or grab any slot here: [CALENDAR_LINK]
- **What burns it:** bounces above 2%; mail failing SPF, DKIM or DMARC.

## 2. LinkedIn DMs (precision play), Tier 1 and 2 only
Judge it on meetings, not replies. (Source cites one platform's 257K sends where AI-personalized messages got more replies but slightly fewer meetings: 0.93 vs 1.02 per 100.)
1. Fix your profile first: headline says who you help and the result, in plain words.
2. Save the 2 or 3 buyers at each Tier 1 and Tier 2 account to a Sales Navigator lead list.
3. **Every morning check:** Sales Navigator "Viewed your profile recently", likes and comments on your posts, "Following your company".
4. **Send the request right after** they notice you, and say so in the note (under 200 characters; for Tier 1 rewrite per person):
> Hi [first name], saw you [viewed my profile / liked my post on [topic] / followed us]. We work with [company type] on [the problem]. Happy to connect.
5. **Message 1 the day after they accept** (lead with something useful):
> Thanks for connecting, [first name]. We just put together [a 1-page note / a teardown] on [the problem] for [company type]. Want me to send it over?
6. **Message 2, 5 days later if no reply:**
> [First name], 1 thing we keep seeing at [company type]: [1 specific pattern]. Happy to send the full note.
7. **When they say "send it":**
> Here it is: [LINK]. Worth 20 minutes to walk through it? [DAY_1 TIME] or [DAY_2 TIME]?
8. Run it as one sequence in [LINKEDIN_SEQUENCER, e.g. lemlist Multichannel] (visit, invite with note, 2 messages). Add profile viewers and new followers by hand each morning.
9. **Withdraw pending requests older than 3 weeks** each week. LinkedIn restricts invites when too many sit pending. Withdrawn people can't be re-invited for up to 3 weeks.
- Benchmarks cited (Reachium, 180,155 requests): 27.1% accepted, 27.6% of those replied, 2.0% booked. About 5 meetings per 1,000 requests.

## 3. Cold calling (Tier 1 closer)
Source numbers: Belkins, 175,000+ dials, about 1 meeting per 370. The author's own team ran about 1 per 37 and it only paid off on seven-figure deals, so he cut the phone for everything below Tier 1.
1. **Check do-not-call and consent rules** for every country on the list before buying mobiles. Get your own legal read.
2. Pull Tier 1 mobiles with [MOBILE_FINDER, e.g. Prospeo via Clay] from each person's LinkedIn URL. Scrub against the do-not-call registry.
3. Load into [DIALER, e.g. Nooks, a parallel dialer]; sync calls to your CRM.
4. **Call the day after email 1** and open on the same situation:
> [First name], it's [your name] at [your company]. I emailed you yesterday about [the situation behind the signal]. Worth 20 minutes next week to walk you through it?
> If "just send me an email": It's already in your inbox, subject line "[SUBJECT]". Can I put 20 minutes on [DAY] so we can go through it together?
5. **Voicemail (15 seconds)** pointing to the email. Stop at 2 voicemails (Gong data cited: email replies went 2.73% to 5.87% with a voicemail, and fell to 2.2% with 3 or more).
> [First name], [your name] from [your company]. I emailed you yesterday about [the situation behind the signal]. No need to call back. You can reply right there.
6. Keep your calendar open and send the invite before you hang up.
7. Log every dial: conversation, pickup without conversation, voicemail, no answer.
- Skip generic title lists: those people get dialed all day and stopped picking up.

## 4. Track and run it
- Friday numbers: email = meetings per 1,000 sent; LinkedIn = meetings per 100 accepted requests; calls = meetings per 100 conversations.
- Change 1 thing at a time, judge on meetings booked.
- 4-week rollout: **Wk 1** domains, DNS, warm-up, LinkedIn profile, do-not-call check. **Wk 2** build list and tiers, save Sales Navigator buyers, write call opener and voicemail. **Wk 3** turn on signals, write the 3 emails, build the sequencer flow, pull and scrub Tier 1 mobiles. **Wk 4** domains are warm, start email for every tier, add LinkedIn people daily, call Tier 1 the day after email 1.

## Guardrails (added, not in source)
- Check email law for each market before sending (CAN-SPAM, GDPR/PECR, the Spam Act in Australia), include opt-out, and honour it.
- LinkedIn's terms restrict automation tools. Review the risk before automating invites and messages, and keep volume modest.
- Send-day email verification and 2% bounce ceiling still apply.

# Not for
- Consumer or local-trade lists (use a Google Maps and license-records list for those).
- Replacing list quality. Fix the list and tiers first.
- Mass-calling without a do-not-call scrub and a legal check.

# Source
- Alex Vacca (@itsalexvacca), X article "How to book meetings with cold email, LinkedIn DMs and cold calling", 26 Oct 2026: https://x.com/itsalexvacca/status/2114749822704193558
- Summary post: https://x.com/itsalexvacca/status/2114856538498363698
- Author is CEO of Frontal (GTM agency) and a Clay Elite Studio Partner, so tool picks (Clay, Prospeo, Instantly, lemlist, Nooks, Sales Navigator) reflect that. Benchmarks and prices are as he quoted them in Oct 2026 from Instantly, Reachium, Belkins and Gong reports. Own-campaign numbers (5 to 18% reply on signal campaigns) are his claims.

# skill: set-up-agent-governance-as-plumbing
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/set-up-agent-governance-as-plumbing.md
========================================================================

---
name: Set up agent governance as plumbing
description: >-
  Use this when a company already has a chatbot acceptable-use policy and now
  needs controls for background agents that write to real systems: provisioned
  accounts, read/propose/write permissions, named owners, a registry, logs that
  include denials, and shadow mode.
---
# Goal
Govern agents by identity, permissions, owners and logs, so you can answer "who changed this?" in minutes and turn any agent off.

# Inputs
- Model-provider API keys, service accounts whose names include AI, bot or GPT, and expenses from model providers
- The first workflow you will take to production
- Named people who can own action types (not a team name)
- Identity provider, audit storage, and a place to keep an agent registry

# Steps
1. Treat current chatbot policy (no confidential data in public tools, approved-app list, an AI council) as coverage for tools people prompt. It does not cover an agent that updates records at 2am.
2. Put five controls in place before any agent may write to a system:
   1. Agents act as a company-provisioned account. No personal API keys or admin accounts. Access starts read-only and grows only to an agreed production scope. The company can revoke it any time.
   2. Separate read, propose and update. Each needs permission from an admin who can revoke it. Check permission at the moment of the action, not only at the start of the run.
   3. Name an owner for each type of action. The workflow says where the agent decides and where a named person decides. Identify that human slice before you build. Example from the article: the AP manager approves vendor bank-detail changes or a new vendor above $25k. Don't assign this to a team.
   4. Register every agent: purpose, owner, users, systems it can access, and version.
   5. Log every action in an append-only, tamper-evident log, including actions the agent wanted to take but was denied. No log, no action: don't dispatch actions unless audit storage is up.
3. Route tool calls, system-of-record calls, model calls, secret reads and outbound messages through one place. On each call, check that agent's allowlist for that environment, read at runtime so a change applies to the next action. If allowed, grant scoped access and log it. If denied, block and log the attempt.
4. Roll out over about 60–90 days:
   - Weeks 1–2: Find all agents, including unapproved ones. Start with the model-provider admin console (API keys), service accounts named AI/bot/GPT, and model-provider expenses.
   - Weeks 2–3: Add every agent to the registry with an owner. If nobody will own it, turn it off.
   - Weeks 3–5: Create three access tiers: sandbox, shared workflow, production. Write down what each may access. Sandboxes get limited credentials, data and tools, plus a person who reviews actions.
   - Weeks 4–6: Pick the first production workflow. Name every action type and a person for each.
   - Weeks 6–10: Run the agent in shadow mode on a real queue, with no write access to systems of record. Record intended actions and have a person review them. The log shows where the agent chose differently from the person.
   - Weeks 10–12: After written sign-off from Risk and IT, allow writes for that workflow only, using the shadow log as evidence. New workflows start with no write access. Workflows that move money always keep a human approval.
   - Monthly after: owners review actions, denials, differences from employees, and token cost. Reserve a budget before each call and deny calls that would exceed it. Retire unused agents.
5. Worked example from the article: start an accounts-payable (AP) agent in a sandbox with temporary credentials and a copy of last quarter's exceptions. When three groups want the same agent, collapse to one agent, one maintained prompt, and the AP manager as process owner. Run it on real exceptions in shadow mode. Then grant write access only to vendor-master fields for bank details and payment terms, and send changes above $25k to the AP manager.
6. Don't let each team build its own agent infrastructure. People closest to the work can invent uses and build agents in a shared sandbox, but accounts, permissions, registry and logs stay shared. Point solutions with their own permission dashboards recreate sprawl.

# Success check
- Every running agent has a provisioned account, an owner, a registry row and a version.
- Writes are blocked unless audit storage is up and the allowlist permits the action.
- Searching the log for a change shows what the agent did, which version, which rule allowed it, who approved it, and any denied attempts.
- The first workflow finished shadow mode before gaining write access.

# Failure modes
- Policy PDFs and councils with no named owners.
- Personal API keys and cards, so nobody can explain token spend.
- Granting write access without a shadow-mode log.
- The 90/10 agent/human split and 60–90 day timeline are the author's guidance from his firm's work with large companies, not a benchmark for yours.

# Anti-patterns
- Governing only chatbot data leakage and ignoring background writes.
- Assigning action ownership to "the finance team" instead of a person.
- Treating a maturity-model slide deck as the controls.
- Skipping human approval on money movement.
- Treating Varick (the author's firm) as a required vendor.

# Source
Thomas (@thmslj), "AI Governance is plumbing", https://x.com/thmslj/status/2118838596816064629, 2026-11-06. The author works at Varick, which sells this implementation.

# skill: ship-30-identical-shorts
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/ship-30-identical-shorts.md
========================================================================

---
name: Ship 30 identical Shorts
description: >-
  Use this when building faceless YouTube Shorts toward a measurable floor —
  lock one cheap template, ship 30 in the same shape, and optimize
  niche/idea/first-frame/pacing/ending in that order.
---
# Steps

1. Define the product shape once and keep it fixed (from source):
   - 65–90 words of script
   - One AI voice, picked once and never changed
   - Stock footage or screen capture
   - Word-by-word captions centered on screen
   - Quiet bed track from the free YouTube Audio Library
   - 25–35 seconds runtime
   - ~20 minutes to make once the template file exists
   - No camera, face, studio, or advanced editing — drag clips into the template

2. Ignore vanity “bar” work that does not move numbers (unique idea theater, personality, 4K fetish, perfect edit, logo, hashtag/time superstition) until the format has a measured floor.

3. Commit to **30 videos in one identical shape**, changing only the topic. Treat early view counts as noise until ~30; ~9 videos is not enough signal. Do not switch formats after a weak video — that restarts the clock.

4. Optimize the five levers **in this order**:
   1. **Who watches** — niche decides CPM before upload one (source cites Americans 25–45 ~$0.25–$0.40 per 1k views vs teens ~$0.05; treat figures as directional from the post, not guaranteed rates).
   2. **The idea** — one flat sentence you’d say at a bus stop. Concrete stakes beat listicle bait that dies by 0:06.
   3. **First frame** — must look different from other first frames in the niche or the thumb scrolls before the writing matters.
   4. **Change every 4–6 seconds** — new information, raised stake, or contradiction. Transition effects do not count.
   5. **Cut the last ~8 seconds** — payoff, then stop. No outro; post-payoff seconds hurt completion rate (what YouTube pays on, per source).

5. Day-one action (do before closing the loop):
   - Open YouTube on a fresh account
   - Search the niche you’ve been sitting on
   - Watch 20 Shorts all the way through; like the good ones
   - Next day the feed surfaces niche outliers — that is the start of research

## Success check

- Template locked; voice/caption/length unchanged across videos
- Topic is the only variable across a run toward 30
- Each short ends on payoff with no outro padding

## Anti-patterns

- Bookmarking guides instead of doing the day-one watch pass
- Changing format after ~9 posts and calling it “iteration”
- Optimizing logos, hashtags, or posting times before niche + idea + first frame + pacing + ending
- Not a general growth-hack or “get rich” skill — only this Shorts production floor test

## Source

- https://x.com/MethodByVid/status/2099815995502436365
- @MethodByVid (Vid), Sep 15, 2026

# skill: ship-9-information-gain-assets-in-under-24-hours
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/ship-9-information-gain-assets-in-under-24-hours.md
========================================================================

---
name: Ship 9 information-gain assets in under 24 hours
description: >-
  Use this when you need unique AI Search / AEO content fast — ship any of nine
  information-gain assets (dashboard screenshots, product walkthrough, specific
  reviews, before/after, named quotes, afternoon tests, first-party stats, real
  competitor tests, dated experiment timelines) in under 24 hours.
---
# Ship 9 information-gain assets in under 24 hours

Add **information gain** to pages and posts so AI Search can cite unique, specific, quantitative facts competitors lack. Ship any of these nine asset types in under a day.

## Goal

Rank for customer-intent keywords in AI Search by publishing content only you can produce: first-party data, real tests, named reviews, and lived competitor experience.

## Inputs

- `[COMPANY]` / product context
- Access to dashboards, reviews, customers, and (ideally) competitor trial accounts
- Privacy review before publishing any first-party usage data

## The 9 assets (pick what you can ship today)

1. **Dashboard screenshots**  
   Show real numbers (anonymized is fine) nobody else can publish.

2. **Short product YouTube walkthrough**  
   Show how it’s used and answer frequent questions on camera.

3. **Real reviews, quoted + screenshotted**  
   Pull from Google / Trustpilot / Reddit. Prefer reviews with specific likes/dislikes — not “loved the product!”

4. **Before/after from a real project**  
   Include numbers, timelines, and screenshots.  
   Example: “We ran this for 30 days and traffic went from X to Y.”

5. **Named customer/client quote**  
   Include name, title, photo, a real opinion. Bonus if it mildly disagrees with the obvious industry take.

6. **Afternoon test you (or the team) can run**  
   Example: ask ChatGPT “what do you think about `[COMPANY]`” for 50 users; publish what happened, interesting data, and correlation with your top users’ AI sentiment scores.

7. **First-party stat**  
   From SaaS usage or similar. Include sample size and analysis methodology. Never publish anything that violates user privacy.

8. **Competitor comparison from real use**  
   Don’t rebuild “[Competitor] vs [Competitor]” from marketing sites. Sign up, run real flows, capture screenshots, pros/cons, and gotchas.  
   Example: “the free plan caps at 3 users and that’s not on the pricing page.”

9. **Dated experiment timeline**  
   List what you tested, outcomes, and dates.  
   Example: “We migrated from WordPress to Framer on March 21st; here’s traffic over the following 90 days.”

## How to run (same day)

1. Pick 1–3 asset types you can finish in &lt;24 hours.  
2. Gather evidence (screenshots, quotes, numbers, trial notes).  
3. Publish on the money page, comparison page, or a dedicated post that links from those pages.  
4. Prefer crawlable HTML (text + images with context) over image-only claims.  
5. Pair with related moves: methodology/competitor scoring tables, About Us key-facts, GSC striking-distance BOFU pages.

## Success check

- Asset includes specifics only you could produce (numbers, names, dates, screenshots, lived UX)  
- Claims are attributable and privacy-safe  
- Published where AI and buyers evaluating the offer will see it

## Anti-patterns

- Generic “trusted by teams worldwide” fluff  
- Reviews or quotes with no specifics  
- Competitor pages written only from their marketing copy  
- Stats with no sample size / method  
- Publishing identifiable user data

## Source

- https://x.com/RobHoffman_/status/2103563185601360095 (@RobHoffman_, 2026-09-25)  
- Related: [Add methodology scoring for AI information gain](sand-workflow:add-methodology-scoring-for-ai-information-gain), [Pull leads from SEO/AEO via GSC striking-distance queries](sand-workflow:pull-leads-from-seo-aeo-via-gsc-striking-distanc), [Optimize About Us for AI search](sand-workflow:optimize-about-us-for-ai-search)

# skill: skirmish-90s-rts-design-checklist
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/skirmish-90s-rts-design-checklist.md
========================================================================

---
name: Skirmish 90s RTS design checklist
description: >-
  Use this when Skirmish pitches, designs or reviews a browser RTS, to check it
  still feels like a 90s real-time strategy game.
---
# Skirmish 90s RTS design checklist

Use this as the design checklist. "In the spirit of" Command & Conquer, Total Annihilation and Age of Empires means the systems and feel, never the assets. No factions, units, names, logos, music, sprites or maps from those games or any other game.

## Economy

One clear loop. Pick per game: harvesters on a finite resource (C&C), metal and energy flow with no gathering unit (Total Annihilation), or workers on food, wood, gold and stone with ages (Age of Empires).

## Base building

A build queue, a placement grid, a power or supply limit, a tech tree that unlocks units and buildings.

## Army control

Drag-select, control groups, right-click move and attack, rally points, waypoints, fog of war and a minimap.

## Combat

Simple counters (a rock-paper-scissors triangle), unit stats players can read, one or two special abilities per faction.

## Presentation

Sidebar or bottom-panel UI, chunky pixel sprites, a 640x480 feel scaled up, a voiced announcer, short briefing screens before missions.

## Modes

Skirmish against an AI first, then a short campaign of two or three missions with objectives.

  control.
---
# Steps

1. Clone the repo (or your fork):
   `git clone https://github.com/block/buzz.git`
2. From the repo root, run the project setup script:
   `./scripts/setup.sh`
   Prerequisites called out in Getting started / Block-internal notes include rustup, bun, node, just, docker; Block folks may also install goose (what Buzz relies on internally).
3. Build:
   `just build-all`
4. After the server/relay is up, add your AI agent to a channel as a teammate (same membership model as a person), set its permissions/scopes, and collaborate in real time. Tweet framing: channels, search, Git, and automations run from the self-hosted workspace.

## Notes from source

- Product tagline: “A workspace where humans and agents build together, on a relay you own.”
- Architecture mentions include Nostr, Postgres, Redis.
- Goose is the related agent runtime Buzz can rely on — not the same as Buzz itself.

## Anti-patterns

- Not a general “how to build an AI business” playbook — only Buzz self-host setup from the source post + README quick start shown in the video
- Do not invent ACL schemas or runtime flags beyond current Buzz docs for your version
- Do not confuse Buzz (workspace/relay) with goose (agent runtime)

# skill: test-whether-ai-assistants-relay-an-ai-only-offe
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/test-whether-ai-assistants-relay-an-ai-only-offe.md
========================================================================

---
name: Test whether AI assistants relay an AI-only offer
description: >-
  Use this when you want to measure which AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT,
  Perplexity) read your site and pass a specific offer or message on to buyers,
  and which page format they pick up best.
---
# Steps

1. **Pick pages AI already cites.** List pages that AI answers already cite or link for your category (check AI answers for buyer questions, or an AEO tracking tool). Pick about `<N_PAGES>` (Ramp used ~50). Ignore Google ranking; one of Ramp's best pages mattered little for Google.
2. **Split into balanced test groups.** One group per format, balanced by each page's existing AI citation volume so groups are comparable:
   - Markdown version of the page
   - Plain stripped-down HTML (no nav or design chrome)
   - Schema-heavy version (structured data injected)
3. **Write the offer for agents.** Address it directly to AI agents. Include the exact offer (`<OFFER>`), the exact claim/booking URL, and step-by-step claim instructions. Give each format and page variant unique tracking (`<TRACKING_PARAM>` or a distinct URL) so any relay maps back to format and page.
4. **Serve it only to bots.** Detect AI crawlers at the edge and serve the variant to them; humans see the unchanged page. Ramp used Cloudflare Workers. Note: some bots pose as normal browsers (Ramp saw DeepSeek appear as a 2017 Chrome version), and Cloudflare's bot categories missed major LLM platforms, so build your own user-agent and IP list too.
5. **Log every AI bot visit.** Record platform, user agent, page and variant served. Expect visits from many AI platforms; in Ramp's test Claude's crawler out-visited all other named AI crawlers combined.
6. **Query the assistants daily.** Each day, ask ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity `<BUYER_QUESTIONS>`: the questions a real prospect asks when choosing a tool in your category. Scan every answer for the offer, the URL and the branded offer name.
7. **Score per model and per format.** Track daily match counts by model, by format and by page. Record how specific each mention is (exact offer and link, vague reference, or none).
8. **Run it for at least 4–5 weeks.** Ramp saw ~40 matches at 2.5 weeks, then a sudden ~4× jump in Claude's daily rate around week 3, 370 matches by day 32 (peak 33 in a day). Perplexity went from vague to the branded name only on day 33. Short tests understate the effect.
9. **Act on the result.**
   - Move winning content to the winning format (Ramp: markdown was the only format that reliably surfaced; schema did not).
   - Plan per model; one "AI" strategy does not work across Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity.
   - Put key messages on pages AI already trusts; low-citation pages got zero mentions in any format.

# Success check
- Each model has a daily match count, a specificity rating and attributed clicks or sign-ups from the tracking parameters.
- You can name the best format and the best pages, with numbers.

# Source
- Original: Ramp Engineering, "Marketing to AI agents": https://engineering.ramp.com/post/marketing-to-ai-agents
- Relayed by CrowdReply (@CrowdReply_io), 9 Nov 2026: https://x.com/CrowdReply_io/status/2119809230861746556
- CrowdReply's post ends in a lead-gen pitch (reply "citations"). All figures are Ramp's own, not independently verified.

# Anti-patterns
- Treating AI-only content as hidden from everyone. Serving bots different content from humans is cloaking under Google's spam policies; keep the bot version factually the same as the human page plus the offer, and accept the search risk knowingly. (added, not in source)
- Offers or claims in the bot version that you can't honour, or that break advertising or financial-promotion rules. (added, not in source)
- Assuming schema markup wins because it is "for machines".
- Judging after one or two weeks.
- Averaging all models into one number.
- Relying only on a CDN's bot categories to spot AI crawlers.
- Putting the offer on pages AI doesn't already cite.

# skill: treat-verification-as-critical-infrastructure
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/treat-verification-as-critical-infrastructure.md
========================================================================

---
name: Treat verification as critical infrastructure
description: >-
  Use this when creating or maintaining an agent verification skill with pstack
  (/create-verification-skill, Build the Lever CLI, Feature Map,
  /maintain-verification-skill), preferring cloud agents over worktrees, or
  using verification in feature/perf/feedback loops.
---
# Steps
1. Treat a high-quality verification skill as critical infrastructure (not "just" a skill): an agent that can verify its own work closes the loop without you as the bottleneck. Done well, it can amplify whole-team output (including non-engineers).
2. Install pstack, then run `/create-verification-skill`. Optionally add Dr Eggbot (ships with pstack) and ask it to create an engineer bot that runs `/create-verification-skill` and sets up a daily routine for `/maintain-verification-skill`.
3. Prefer a tech stack / runtime that agents can interact with and debug (e.g. Electron/web via Chrome DevTools Protocol; iOS simulator). If the runtime is poor, ask the agent to create tools (e.g. lldb, or a custom sidecar package) or use what you have — [PLACEHOLDER: exact tool list for your stack]. Agentic verification is important enough that building rich debugging tools or choosing a different stack may be worth it.
4. Apply "Build the Lever": prefer giving agents tools rather than just markdown. For verification, create a small CLI that scripts interaction and debugging of your app in an agent-friendly utility (fewer tokens than throwaway click scripts; more reproducible and testable).
5. Design the agent-friendly CLI with these properties (from the extract):
   - API easy to compose (deep modules)
   - Potentially destructive commands have `--dry-run`
   - Subcommands for gradual disclosure
   - Descriptive error messages that say what to do instead
   - Rich `--help` text
   - Machine-readable output (e.g. JSON)
6. Also cover dev experience the CLI should support: seeding a dev database; auth / test users / API calls against test/staging; installing and bringing up the dev environment consistently. Keep the CLI well maintained and tested. Spend time making it good and error-free before advanced work. Hypothetical Electron CLI command examples: [PLACEHOLDER — media in source; not transcribed]. Other example commands: [PLACEHOLDER — media in source; not transcribed].
7. Prefer Cursor cloud agents over local git worktrees for parallelism after the verification skill can land a few PRs:
   - Worktrees: high storage/resources; limited parallel agents on one machine.
   - Cloud agents: real computer; install deps; run app; videos/screenshots; interact like a user. Set up cloud environment (first-build agent help; then snapshot for fast subsequent starts). [PLACEHOLDER: exact cloud environment setup commands for your repo].
8. Create a Feature Map (searchable map of features, what they do, how to get there from a user's perspective):
   - `/create-verification-skill` auto-creates `references/features` alongside a README.md (the map: high-level overview with links to details). Mention Feature Map files in the verification SKILL.md.
   - Agents catalog the app for you — don't write these yourself initially.
   - Treat as "materialized memory": compact form of codebase truth designed to save tokens; shared markdown inside the skill benefits all contributors.
   - Example feature entry shape: [PLACEHOLDER — media in source; not transcribed]. Example verification skill: https://github.com/poteto/verification-skill-example
9. Maintain continuously: run `/maintain-verification-skill` at least once a day so agents have latest control details. Agents may update Feature Map while working; `/maintain-verification-skill` catches what is missed. Keep improving the CLI; invest like critical infra (optional: oncall rotation on it).
10. Usage patterns (with `/poteto-mode`; in Cursor, Opt+Enter on autocomplete can pin `/poteto-mode` as a Custom Mode so the agent is reminded every turn):
    - New features: `/poteto-mode build <description of feature, any useful context>. use /control-app to verify your changes and show me a video and screenshots as proof` (`/control-app` = result of `/create-verification-skill`). In Grok @Bot: spawn a cloud agent to do the same (keeps bot context clean; bot as coordinator).
    - Perf: `spawn a cloud agent to use /poteto-mode to improve the initial loading time of our app. first use /control-app to take a trace of the status quo, and identify opportunities for improvement. then do a targeted fix and use /control-app + a /swarm to confirm the win` (`/swarm` fans out cloud agents to run verification for sample size / fuzz / no-regression).
    - User reports: put verification inside Grok @Bot routines or Cursor Automations (schedule or event). Pipe feedback (e.g. Slack); bots try to reproduce with a cloud agent; if Feature Map/verification is good enough, optionally auto-fix.

## Anti-patterns
- Treating verification as a one-off skill instead of maintained infrastructure.
- Giving agents only markdown instead of a Build-the-Lever CLI.
- Jumping to advanced verification before the CLI is good and error-free.
- Preferring local worktrees for multi-agent parallelism when cloud agents are available after a solid verification/dev setup.
- Letting the Feature Map go stale (skip daily `/maintain-verification-skill`).
- Choosing/keeping a tech stack that is hard to debug and control without investing in agent-usable tooling.

## Source
- https://x.com/poteto/status/2094457600259842065, @poteto, Mon Aug 31 16:09:39 +0000 2026 (2026-09-01 02:09 AEST)

# skill: turn-launch-post-replies-into-personalized-produ
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/turn-launch-post-replies-into-personalized-produ.md
========================================================================

---
name: Turn launch-post replies into personalized product demos
description: >-
  Use this when launching a product on X whose output can be personalized
  (video, image, copy, audit) and you want the reply section to become a live
  demo that drives signups.
---
# Turn launch-post replies into personalized product demos

## Why it works
X ranks posts that keep people on the platform. Long reply threads and time spent in the comments push a post further. Every personalized result posted in the replies is a public demo, which makes the next person ask for one too.

## Steps
1. **Pick the personalization.** Choose one thing your product can make for a single person in about a minute: [OUTPUT, e.g. a video of them in a movie scene].
2. **Write the hook reply.** Answer "congrats"-type comments with a question that collects the input. Example: "Thanks! What's your favorite movie? I'll make you something cool."
3. **Wire the pipeline:**
   - The X API reads new replies on the launch post.
   - Claude turns each reply (plus profile context) into a generation prompt: [PROMPT_TEMPLATE].
   - [PRODUCT_API] generates the result.
   - The X API posts a reply with a preview and a link.
4. **Gate the full result.** Reply "Your [OUTPUT]'s ready, go check it out" with a preview and a link to [RESULT_PAGE]. The full result is waiting on your site, and editing or keeping it requires signing up.
5. **Personalize onboarding.** After signup, tailor the experience to their name, company and what they asked for.
6. **Let it compound.** Every public preview invites more requests. Watch the comment-to-like ratio and time in the replies as signs it's working.

## Guardrails (added, not in source)
- Only use someone's photo or likeness if they explicitly asked, and say upfront what you'll make.
- Automated replies should go only to people who replied to you. Rate-limit them, avoid duplicate text, and follow X's automation rules and API tier limits.
- Have a human review outputs before they post, and plan capacity, since the source says launches have broken products under load.

## Gaps
The source's 10-page setup guide is gated. Exact X API endpoints, prompt templates and queue design are [PLACEHOLDER].

## Not for
Products with no fast, personalizable output, or cold auto-replies to people who didn't engage.

## Source
Matt Epstein (@mattepstein, Shown Media), "I drove $7M by abusing X's API and connecting it to Claude", https://x.com/mattepstein/status/2112573983707247036, 21 Oct 2026 AEDT. The $7M figure is the author's claim, and the article ends with a pitch for his agency.

# skill: turn-pr-smells-into-lasting-rules
# url: https://retrend.github.io/grok-skill-library/skills/turn-pr-smells-into-lasting-rules.md
========================================================================

---
name: Turn PR smells into lasting rules
description: >-
  Use this when acting as codebase gardener — watching the PR stream for
  recurring smells and converting each weed into a rule or hard constraint so
  agent-era slop cannot grow back.
---
# Steps
1. Assign (or act as) a gardener: someone quietly watching the stream of PRs into the codebase, noticing smells (examples from the extract: the third `isRecord` this week; lint suppressions creeping like ivy).
2. Tend weeds steadily: every weed you pull becomes a rule so it cannot grow back. With careful grooming the codebase stays a garden; without that, it is just whatever grew.
3. Prefer organic architecture foundations over soft guidance alone:
   - Good codebases have strong foundations and constraints (these files go here; this kind of code goes there) — historically via conventional frameworks/languages for the lowest common denominator, or a style guide enforced by code review.
   - Infinite agent "monkeys with keyboards" obsolete style-guide-only enforcement. Codebases designed for agents need hard constraints so even the dumbest agent (and pilot) can contribute meaningfully.
4. Invest where impact is highest (per extract): refactoring the codebase and choosing a tech stack with strong type systems / compiler diagnostics has far greater impact than AGENTS.md and tweaking skills. Hard constraints and well thought-out architecture guide agents to do the right thing by default. The best rules are in your code.
5. Encode each recurring smell as a durable constraint — [PLACEHOLDER: lint rule / type / CI check / compiler diagnostic chosen for your stack] — so the same weed cannot return.

## Anti-patterns
- Leaving PR smells unchecked until the garden is engulfed in slop.
- Relying mainly on AGENTS.md and skill tweaks instead of hard constraints, architecture, and typed/compiler-backed rules in code.
- Expecting code review style guides alone to tame agent-scale contribution volume.

- https://x.com/poteto/status/2090546476464451907, @poteto, Thu Aug 20 21:08:15 +0000 2026 (2026-08-21 07:08 AEST)
